A well-formed bounding box has distinct lateral sides and low/high edges; every obstacle point must lie inside it. This is point motion in a 2D scene, without finite robot shape, dynamics, sensors or uncertain coordinates. §2.1/5.1, pp.3–4/11: proofs assume a Mathematical Components real field, with exact arithmetic and boolean equality/order. Rational numbers suffice; no completeness of the real numbers is required. The generic executable accepts a number type, four arithmetic operations and two comparisons. Its user must instantiate them consistently with field laws. Ordinary floating point does not satisfy that exact model; no rounding-error theorem is given. §2.1, pp.4–5: a determinant computes signed area for above/below/collinear tests using ring operations. Vertical-cylinder tests ensure projections lie within segment x range. Vertical projection is the only operation using division, returning an option outside its range. The edge_below relation is transitive for outgoing edges sharing a left endpoint, but is not a global partial order. §2.2/5.4.1, pp.5/13: cells store low/high edges and ordered unique left/right boundary point lists. Closed cells have both sides; open cells have no right side yet. Safe part consists of strict interior plus lateral points strictly between low/high edges excluding recorded unsafe points. Owned part excludes bottom and left boundaries, allowing unique ownership even when cells meet. Safety is not a claim that every boundary point is free. §§3–4, pp.5–8: scan state stores vertically arranged open cells as prefix/last/suffix, closed cells with the last one separate, and cached last x/high edge. Initial processing needs a first event strictly beyond the left boundary to construct a first closed cell. Event preparation uses insertion sort merging equal positions, then separately sorts outgoing edges when processing each event. Recursion consumes the finite event list; no asymptotic complexity theorem is reported. §4, pp.6–8: event order is lexicographic in x then y. Four branches distinguish x advance, same x above the last high edge, same x below it, and same x on it. Same-x handling updates/discards would-be zero-width cells and preserves old unsafe-side points. Vertical alignment of separate events is supported, while vertical obstacle segments remain excluded. §4.5/second_phase_safety, pp.9–10: eight prerequisites are well-formed box, permitted endpoint-only intersections among boundaries/edges, inside-box events, strict lexicographic event ordering, outgoing edges starting at their event, later events covering right endpoints, no event in an edge interior, and duplicate-free outgoing lists. Each resulting cell has center strictly inside, well-formed side lists and safe part disjoint from unsafe events/edges. Isolated events are supported by this more general contract. §4.5/two_phase_safety, p.10: composing preparation with processing reduces prerequisites to well-formed box, unique edges, endpoint-only intersections including box edges, and all edge points inside the box. The conclusion gives interior center, side well-formedness and obstacle avoidance for every returned cell. Input preparation must preserve the original edges, since safety relative only to the generated event set could otherwise omit an obstacle. §5.1, p.11: generic_trajectories avoids Mathematical Components structures and drops the dependent edge proof field for extraction. Proof files instantiate this same generic algorithm with field operations via notations and generalize theorems across sections. Rational implementation uses integer numerator/positive denominator. No verified foreign-function wrapper, machine-integer overflow proof or independent extraction replay is provided in this reading. §5.2, pp.11–12: six nested invariant groups describe open cells/remaining events; cache consistency and event/edge relationships; special last open cell; disjointness/nonempty cells; coverage of processed obstacles by high boundaries; and safe lateral-side exclusions. A preliminary proof under no vertically aligned events verified fewer branches; the main result described here is the stronger proof including degeneracies. §5.3, pp.12–13: pairwise order of all earlier/later open-cell high edges replaces relying on adjacent sortedness under a nontransitive relation. Projection comparisons require the point x coordinate to be in both edge cylinders. These assumptions make local geometric order reasoning sound. §5.4, pp.13–15: unique owned parts and coverage of each processed obstacle by cell high boundaries imply interior safety by contradiction. An interior point on an obstacle would belong to its own cell and a distinct boundary-covering cell. Separate invariants show events appear in side lists, and inherited side hazards survive degenerate replacements. Disjoint ownership does not imply closed cells have no shared boundary. §§1/6.1, pp.3/16–17: proof does not establish union of owned parts covers the box or that adjacent cells with a safe passage share a represented door. Tests reportedly support both properties, with no described count/distribution/ground truth. Missing either could cause the application to miss an existing path. Per-cell nonemptiness does not prove the output list is nonempty or complete. §6, pp.16–17: integration in a larger path tool assesses usability, but path search, smoothing with Bezier curves and full trajectory proof are outside this paper. Proof effort is almost 15000 lines in 12 files. No runtime, memory, compilation time, hardware, systematic benchmark or independently reproduced build is reported. - FRAIG-BMC (2025)
    - title: FRAIG-BMC: Functional Reduction to Speed Up Bounded Model Checking
    - what: Introduces FRAIG-BMC, an on-the-fly functional-reduction procedure integrated into each BMC unrolling. It simplifies trivial logic, reuses structurally hashed nodes, and SAT-checks simulation-equivalent nodes before CNF encoding, reducing variables and clauses while preserving the BMC property check. The algorithm maintains an unrolled-AIG-node to SAT-variable map and performs three ordered reductions: constant/idempotent AND simplification, structural hashing, then simulation equivalence classes checked by SAT. Equivalences are checked across time frames, which a standalone pre-BMC FRAIG cannot exploit. For constrained properties Ck, the paper adds filtered random simulation over the constraint cone of influence and a SAT-sampling alternative with blocking clauses and optional random unit clauses. Large equivalence classes are capped and treated as unique to avoid excessive checking. The implementation extends AIGER aigbmc with CaDiCaL and compares it to CaDiCaL-backed baseline and ABC-BMC3 on SEC, partial-retention (PartRet), and information-flow (IFC) benchmarks.
    - number: SEC Table I includes 17 named cases; FRAIG-BMC reaches bound 243 on i2c and 907 on ss pcm
    - number: SEC cases show hundreds of thousands to over one million trivial/structural merges (e.g., des3 area 597,798 trivial and 1,069,415 structural)
    - number: time limit 3,600 seconds; server Intel Xeon 8375C, 256 GB memory
    - number: PartRet 61 cases and IFC 56 cases according to figure captions
    - limits: The method targets bit-level AIG transition systems and safety properties checked to finite bounds; it does not establish unbounded safety. Functional equivalence is relative to the current simulation candidates and then validated by SAT, while constrained simulation assumes constraints can be represented and sampled from their cone. An excessively large equivalence class is deliberately not fully checked, trading possible reductions for runtime. Benchmarks contain repeated circuit copies and all runs use a 3,600-second timeout on one 256-GB Xeon server, so gains may depend on structural redundancy and hardware.

    - what: Introduces functional probabilistic invariants—inequalities of the form E[h] ≤ h(c) over distributions of program states—to verify tail bounds directly for the randomized CVM distinct-elements streaming algorithm, and mechanizes both the original and a new total unbiased variant in Isabelle/HOL.     - title: A Formal Verification Approach to Safeguard Controller Variables from Single Event Upset
    - what: Defines conditionally relevant variables (CRVs): variables whose single-event-upset bit flip can change a controller safety-property result. Strong normalization does not by itself state one uniform numeric bound or asymptotic runtime, especially for general nondeterministic branching. §4, p.10: ordinary partial WP puts recursive continuation under later; guarded Banach fixpoint requires contractiveness rather than positivity. Löb induction may prove partial wp of a diverging program with false postcondition because it never returns. Removing later and using least fixpoint changes termination obligations; total implies partial, reverse does not follow. §4, p.10: invariant-opening for total correctness is limited to timeless assertions; general nested invariants/WP-containing assertions cannot be opened unrestrictedly without later. Landin’s knot demonstrates why the restriction matters. Logic supports limited ghost state/invariants/concurrency, not full usual Iris reasoning power for total correctness. §4, p.10: concurrent total WP requires termination for every scheduler. Busy waiting that terminates only under fair scheduling cannot be verified. Paper explicitly leaves fair scheduler integration for future work; no distributed-protocol liveness or eventual network-delivery assumption is supplied. §5.1, pp.11–12: command parses familiar Inductive syntax as raw bound-variable-aware terms, turns top-level constructor wands into separating conjuncts, binders into existentials, cases into disjunctions, abstracts parameters/recursion/indices, replaces recursive calls with rec, turns the constructor conclusion into index-equality constraints, and simplifies trivial equalities. Higher-order abstract syntax helps binder substitution. Rocq elaborates holes and type-checks resulting declarations. §§5.1–5.2, pp.12–13: generated curried fixpoints avoid tuple plumbing and recognize required nonexpansive OFE morphisms for higher-order predicate arguments. Signature relations live in iProp; combinators express equality, wand, persistent relation, contravariance flip and respectful function relation. Proper instances in Rocq typeclasses make monotonicity extensible beyond a fixed syntactic positivity checker. §5.2, p.13: solver normalizes quantifiers/wands/modalities, then closes equal terms, applies hypotheses or searches signature/Proper rule and recurses. It is goal-directed proof generation, not complete decision procedure for monotonicity. New nested predicates may need manual instances; improved automation/errors are future work. §5.3, pp.13–14: IPM separates persistent and spatial named hypotheses. Proving object-logic wand is not a Rocq lambda introduction; tactics apply derived context-manipulation lemmas. Elpi port manages typed holes, controls typeclass resolution, reduces context functions and checks fresh names. It reimplements selected Ltac wrappers because bridge changes contexts inefficiently; declarations remain subject to Rocq validation. §§5.4–5.5/7, pp.15/17: Elpi database records generated induction theorem, parameter/constructor counts; iInduction queries it and opens case hypotheses. Prototype2106LOC=345Rocq+1761Elpi. Evaluation redefines totalWP and derives its existing proof rules without changing user signatures; no runtime timings, proof-speed comparison, broad benchmark suite or user study. Production integration unresolved due partial duplicated IPM wrappers. §§6–7, pp.16–17: native Rocq Inductive can target unfolded heap->Prop predicates but not Iris’s Sigma-bundled iProp arity; this is not a universal impossibility for all separation logic embeddings. Mere semantic positivity/monotonicity is more general than syntactic strict positivity, with no real-life strictness-gap case claimed. Source code is archived but not built here; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation.

- LeanLTL (2025)
    - title: LeanLTL: A Unifying Framework for Linear Temporal Logics in Lean
    - what: Presents a Lean 4 temporal-logic library with a shared semantic representation for finite and infinite nonempty traces, arbitrary Lean propositions/data expressions, LTL-like macro notation, and preliminary simplification-based automation. Gives machine-checked embeddings of LTL and LTLf and a traffic-light safety/liveness example. Trace uses an Option-valued sequence N→Option σ, extended natural length, nonemptiness proof, and a proof that values are defined exactly before length. TraceSet is a predicate on traces; TraceFun maps a trace to Option α, with strong/weak get interpreting undefined values as False/True. The LLTL macro recursively rewrites host connectives, pushes next into trace-function arrows, binds strong gets before weak gets, and coerces remaining propositions/predicates into trace sets. The push_ltl simp set translates satisfaction into first-order semantics so existing Lean tactics can finish arithmetic obligations; Figure 1 proves an invariant of the recurrence n=5 initially and n_next=n² by globally_induction and nlinarith. LTL/LTLf embeddings use inductive syntax, evaluation, translation, and a satisfaction-equivalence theorem. The traffic-light example includes queue arithmetic and environment assumptions, proving exactly one light green globally and both lights green infinitely often for traces satisfying those assumptions.

- Nanopass Back-Translation of Call-Return Trees for Mechanized Secure Compilation Proofs (2025)
    - what: Rocq-verified back-translation from a finite well-formed collection of finite call/return trace prefixes into generated source whole programs sharing a context. Organizes the construction as initialization plus four small compiler passes over call-return trees, using identifiers, ghost call stacks and flattened rules before code generation. Proves each requested prefix can be produced by the back-translated source program. Handles stateful, arbitrarily reentrant callbacks and returns separated from their calls by nested interactions. Private loc, is_call and res distinguish external callbacks from internal recursion and recover the correct branch after a return. Separates determinacy and stack invariants across intermediate semantics, then relates ghost locations/stacks to concrete memory/frames. Gives an informal path to stronger finite-relational security, while explicitly leaving integration into a complete compilation-chain security theorem unmechanized.
    - limits: Inputs are finite sets/lists of finite prefixes satisfying well-formedness, including deterministic context behavior: after the same visible history, a context in control cannot choose two different outgoing events. The exact well-formedness predicate is not reproduced. Arbitrary incompatible trace collections are not covered. Compartment interaction uses well-bracketed calls/returns with integer payloads, private state and procedures/interfaces. The exposition assumes one procedure per compartment; the actual development supports multiple procedures and records procedure identifiers in call events. Fine-grained sharing of secure data/code pointers is future work. Theorem3 establishes inclusion of each requested finite prefix in generated-program behavior. It neither states equality of all trace sets nor forbids extra generated behavior, and it does not establish infinite-trace/liveness properties. Finite-prefix witness preservation must not be inflated to arbitrary hyperproperty preservation. The proven artifact is the back-translation and its pass simulations, not a new full RFrSP theorem for the existing compiler or compartmentalized CompCert. Figure1 describes an adaptation requiring forward/backward compiler correctness, separate compilation and recomposition. §1 explicitly says mechanization of that integration is not yet done; §8 makes realistic SECOMP integration future work. RFrSP quantifies finite families of possibly different programs under one target context, requiring one shared source context for the corresponding prefixes. RSP has only one program/prefix. Pointwise independent source contexts would not meet the stronger quantifier order. The informal implication to full abstraction is qualified in §3.1 as a variant of the security-relevant direction, not an unconditional complete fully abstract compiler theorem. It relies on the chosen trace/context/source-target models and the remaining compilation-chain proof. Back-translation constructs whole source programs: a common context depends on the entire trace family, while each generated program depends on its own trace. It does not directly translate the syntax of an arbitrary low-level adversary or prove that every original source program already behaves like the generated replacement. Adding ghost-state conditions to intermediate semantics is justified by forward simulations, not by simply assuming invariants in the final source semantics. Proof obligations include initialization and invariant-preserving matching steps; finite-prefix simulations permit stuttering without establishing divergence preservation. Reuse across languages and proof-effort improvements are author expectations/experience reports. No controlled comparison of developer time, proof checking time, memory, runtime of generated contexts, scale benchmark or LLM-agent result is reported. Prover/library axioms were not audited by this reader.

    - what: A network-specific decision-diagram library factors Boolean network state by fields. Each NDD node branches on a whole field and each edge labels allowed field values with a BDD; reduced ordered NDDs merge equal residual functions. Per-field atomization replaces label BDD operations with atom-set operations, and an incremental update API splits affected atoms. A paper induction proves intended canonicity for fixed field grouping/order; Java integration into five verifiers measures time/memory, including packet rewriting and link-failure models. Benefits rely on field locality and are not uniform across workloads. Records three reduction rules, exclusive/exhaustive edge semantics, field/bit-order assumptions and full canonicity construction, atom minimality and update precondition, complete apply/exist/atomize/update algorithms and qualified listing concerns, hash/GC/cache/implicit-false details, all eight tables and complete scope of empirical results. Separates representation canonicity from implementation correctness and end-to-end network verification, and identifies workload, baseline and source-count discrepancies.

NDDs can still grow exponentially and a node can have up to2^n outgoing edges for an n-bit field; pairwise apply may compare m×n successors. §3.3/AppendixC: Fixed grouping of consecutive bit variables into fields and fixed field order, plus canonical BDD labels with fixed internal bit order, underpin canonicity. Equivalent Boolean functions yield one reduced graph under these conventions; claim does not establish minimum graph size across groupings/orders or efficient construction in worst case. AppendixC proof: Generalize Shannon expansion by partitioning first-field assignments according to equal residual functions, recursively represent residuals, label each equivalence class with its BDD and merge equal successors. This is handwritten mathematical proof, not mechanized code refinement. §3.3 Definition1/AppendixC qualification: Formal edge conditions require disjoint/exhaustive labels but do not explicitly forbid false (empty) labels. Uniqueness argument chooses B1∈label(eu), implicitly requiring every retained edge nonempty.     - what: Defines P4LTL temporal properties over completed packet processings while retaining register state between packets. Models arbitrary input packets and changing table actions, optionally constrained by symbolic control-plane assumptions. Constructs a Büchi transaction product in which the specification automaton advances only at packet return, reducing violations to fair feasible traces. A proof sketch establishes the abstract correspondence; p4tv implements P4-to-Boogie translation, ghost instrumentation and an Ultimate Automizer extension. Evaluation checks19 temporal tasks on nine programs plus assertion checks/scaling, identifying two naturally occurring property failures and three injected defects. Records exact packet-boundary/old/free-variable semantics, register initialization and control-plane scope, product transitions/acceptance and proof-sketch qualifications, refinement algorithm and implementation trust, all Table2/3 cells, actual versus injected bug distinction, p4v approximation and assertion instrumentation, rapid scaling growth, and source specification/prose inconsistencies including vacuous liveness formula. Table applications are nondeterministic action choices. This abstracts a single programmed switch; no proof of interleaved pipeline concurrency, simultaneous register read/modify/write races, multiple switches, queue dynamics or actual hardware refinement is supplied. Packet time is not wall-clock time. §§2/3/7/8: Register initialization is part of each verification configuration. P4NIS failing task9 leaves count unconstrained; successful invariant/assertion examples assume valid/zero initialization or add recovery logic. Persistent arbitrary initial values differ from independently re-randomizing registers every packet. Results under initialization assumptions do not show a real deployment meets those assumptions. §§3.2/4: CPI constrains table keys/actions/parameters, allows symbolic sets of entries and changes between packets. Empty CPI permits every modeled rule. Property checked is assumption implies desired property; it can hold if assumption is impossible. Authors do not report systematic assumption satisfiability/vacuity checks or prove a real controller always enforces CPI. Table2 needs CPI for tasks6,7,8,16 only. §4.1: Predicates are evaluated at packet boundaries: terms normally after processing; old(t) at ingress start after parsing; valid(h) records validity after parsing, hit/apply record occurrence during processing. old(key) and old(para) expressly arbitrary. fwd(t) is egress_spec==t syntactic sugar, so packet-output/architecture correspondence matters. Free variables describe nondeterministic values intended to cover all names; scope/stability must be preserved when translating specifications. §§4/6/7.2: Boundary-only temporal properties can miss transient within-packet violations. Assertion checks use a shadow variable initialized true per packet and capture the assertion at its program point, then check its boundary value. This is an explicit instrumentation workaround; the native P4LTL language still cannot directly observe arbitrary internal events. Correct instrumentation and all relevant visits are part of the trust boundary. §5.1: Product keeps program/specification location pairs, updates specification only on TR(s), uses assume true on other statements, and accepting locations require spec acceptance plus TE/TR boundary.     - what: CompCert extension implementing and verifying a partial control-flow linearization transformation for an acyclic, call-free, initially memory-free subset of C/RTL. Intermediate PredRTL keeps original and transformed program counters to prove semantic preservation via postdominance. A taint analysis and new influence-region proof establish secret-independent control-flow traces at PredRTL. Separates semantic preservation, operation-definedness and two-execution control-flow security. Uses detour postdominance to align live states; instructions on dummy detours execute but discard effects, requiring safe defined operands. PCFL assumes a secret_cond labeling and guarantees a topological transformed graph, one successor at each secret condition, and detour_spec: each original edge v→w maps to v→detour(v,w), with w postdominating the new target. Postdominance alone needs progress/definedness and acyclicity to justify reaching the original target. Dummy PredRTL states preserve architectural register values but still evaluate operations/conditions, which must succeed. Safe operations on typed defined arguments must return a defined value; all registers are initialized to typed defaults. Safety/condition/progress lemmas have only been proved for x86, according to §3.3. CompCert semantic preservation permits improvement of source undefined behavior; it is not exact equivalence for every undefined source execution. Taint selection is irrelevant to preservation provided PCFL/operation premises hold; security additionally needs correct secret labeling and taint invariants. Control-flow security compares runs of the same transformed function with equal public parameters and arbitrary secret parameters, preserving equal public registers and equal program-point traces at equal trace lengths. It addresses control decisions, not constant runtime of individual operations, cache/data-access behavior, microarchitecture or leakage from output values. PredRTL security is proved; §4.2 explicitly says the cube simulation carrying security to SelRTL/RTL is not written. §7 says integration through downstream CompCert assembly passes is future work. Semantic simulation alone does not establish preservation of this two-run security property. Predication implements live/dummy state in a fresh v_orig_reg plus scratch registers, updating with select. Selects are assumed constant-time in the motivating account; x86 builtins are used. Bit-mask lowering is a suggested alternative with 0/1 conditions, not a machine-level constant-time proof. Security transfer would need to treat introduced registers as secret. §5 critical-register relaxation is neither implemented nor proved. Its proof-of-concept Iload extension explicitly assumes axiomatically that any successful load returns a value other than Vundef. This qualification must accompany claims about memory support; no sound arbitrary-memory guarantee is established. §7 proposals for shadow memory, safe division, function calls, global taint and uniform-exit loops are future work. - POPACheck: A Model Checker for Probabilistic Pushdown Automata (2025)
    - what: POPACheck translates finite-data recursive probabilistic MiniProb programs to probabilistic operator precedence automata and checks LTL plus a stack-aware POTL fragment. A support-chain semi-algorithm distinguishes positive nontermination from positively almost-sure termination using numerical upper bounds and expected-runtime certificates. Separated formula automata avoid determinization; experiments cover nested conditioning, games, branching populations and finite-array randomized search. Explains why numerical approximations alone cannot decide exact probability one, how finite expected time is stronger than almost-sure termination, why conditioned support-chain edges need probability ratios, and how stack-aware properties differ from ordinary trace order. Preserves finite data versus unbounded stack, incomplete decisions, all measured rows, two quantitative timeouts, approximate probabilities, formula/code mismatches and absent cross-tool comparison.
    - limits: §§1–2,4: pOPA is a subclass of probabilistic pushdown automata with finite control states and label-driven stack actions, while its induced Markov chain has unbounded stack configurations. MiniProb integers have a chosen finite bit width and arrays fixed size. Arbitrary chosen width does not mean unbounded integer values in a single model. Recursion/nested query depth can be unbounded; this is not arbitrary unbounded array or concurrent distributed-state verification. §2.1/Definition1: precedence matrix is total over labels; bottom symbol # yields to all program labels, so first move pushes. Push records current state/label, shift changes the top label, pop depends on current and saved state. The extra pop-label condition preserves precedence compatibility. Precedence relations are not assumed reflexive/transitive orders. These restrictions enable synchronized stack-aware formula products; do not replace the model by unrestricted pPDA and assume identical algorithms. §§1–2: observe failure rejects and restarts the current query. obs unwinds only to nearest qry boundary, preserving outer queries, so nested posterior sampling is modeled. A conditioning event of zero probability gives an ill-defined query, not an ordinary normalized posterior. Markov probabilities model specified sampling distributions; no adversarial scheduler or Markov decision-process strategy synthesis is evaluated. §2.2: supported logic is LTL and POTL_fχ, not all POTL. Atomic propositions include program events/function names and finite-variable arithmetic tests. Directional next and chain-future/until operators move through procedure frames. Call-return/postcondition matching can be context-free and beyond LTL. Full formal semantics/proofs are referred to [10,40], not fully redeveloped or mechanized here. §3.1: termination triple probabilities are least nonnegative fixed-point solutions of a monotone nonlinear polynomial system. Nontermination at node c is 1 minus the sum of termination outcomes. Support-chain states include only c with strictly positive nontermination; division by that positive quantity conditions push/shift/support probabilities. Support edges summarize finite nested runs. This chain captures limit behavior with the intended probabilistic construction, not a claim that all time-indexed observations can be erased without the formula-aware machinery. §3.1: upper bounds on termination give lower bounds on nontermination. A positive lower bound includes the node. Otherwise the algorithm tries a stronger certificate: stack symbol popped with probability one in finite expected time (PAST). A valid linear expected-time solution implies almost-sure termination (AST), excluding the node. Failure to prove PAST is inconclusive, not nontermination. AST with infinite expected time can fail this stronger test; no total decision procedure is claimed. §3.1: zero variables are removed through value iteration; decomposed Newton computes lower bounds. Upper bounds either satisfy lower<=v<=lower+epsilon and v>=f(v) in Z3, or come from optimistic value iteration initialized at the lower bound. SCC decomposition solves bottom-up. Exact epsilon, stopping tolerance, rational/floating implementation details and independent certificate validation protocol are not supplied in this tool paper, so printed approximate probabilities are not exact certified decimal values. §3.2: separated Büchi/omega-operator-precedence automata have disjoint languages from distinct starting states, allowing synchronized products without determinization. Qualitative checks analyze product SCCs; quantitative checks solve additional support-probability equations with OVI. Theoretical claims: singly exponential time in formula size, polynomial space in pOPA size for qualitative theory, and EXPSPACE for quantitative model checking, citing [40]. These are not guarantees that the implemented semi-algorithm terminates on every valid input. §4: function parameters pass by value or value-result; actual value-result arguments must be variable identifiers. Boolean operators treat zero as false. Bernoulli(e1,e2) has success probability e1/e2; Uniform(e1,e2) is stated half-open [e1,e2). Distributions need valid parameters; general C/Rust overflow, pointer aliasing and undefined behavior are not analyzed. Fig6 supports while, recursion, query and observe, not arbitrary source-language execution. §5: benchmark has three nested-query programs and 16 distinct Q formulas, yielding 20 program/formula rows, plus Sherwood with four S formulas and varied finite sizes. This is a demonstration suite, not a random production corpus. AMD 8-core 4.5GHz,64GB,Ubuntu24.04; one-hour timeout. PReMo/Pray are excluded because they only compute termination probabilities, which OVI handles below one second here. §5/Table3: all three OVI upper-bound runs are below one second, but Z3 times out on Schelling/Virus. Thus the blanket below-one-second prose concerns the chosen successful method, not every attempted solver. A probability-one property may still admit measure-zero violating runs; do not equate AS with all-run deterministic correctness. §5/Schelling: two agents cannot communicate but know each other’s preferences perfectly. p controls recursion and its distribution is fixed to make the model AST.     - title: PoWER Never Corrupts: Tool-Agnostic Verification of Crash Consistency and Corruption Detection
    - what: PoWER encodes crash consistency as a precondition on each storage write: every durable state introduced by a partial write must be permitted by a ghost permission. Prophecy-based storage views and recovery-equivalent writes simplify proofs. A bounded-bit corruption model and an eight-byte corruption-detecting Boolean support atomic data/checksum updates. CapybaraKV in Verus and CapybaraNS in Dafny demonstrate the method, with coarse concurrent KV variants and performance comparisons. Records exact permission quantification, prophecy flush semantics, state versus transition and blanket versus single-use permissions, all four write strategies and concurrency restrictions. Includes correspondence-proof trust boundaries, CRC corruption bounds, Tick-Tock counterexample and CDB protocol, full type/LOC/startup/resource tables, all workload setups and adverse performance cases. Separates conditional detection from arbitrary-media-error recovery and reported proofs from independent proof replay.

    - limits: Core technique requires Hoare pre/postconditions, ghost variables and quantification over crash states. Each asynchronous write requires all chunk-wise old/new durable outcomes to satisfy its permission; executable annotations erase. Soundness depends on every actual storage mutation using the controlled API, correctness of the storage model and a meaningful allowed-recovery predicate. A permission that allows all states proves no useful crash property. Natural storage semantics distinguish readable last-written bytes from outstanding writes. Atomic persistence chunks can survive independently until flush. The prophecy model instead stores read_state and one prophesized durable_state; write updates all readable bytes and chooses a subset of chunk subwrites for durable state. Flush constrains these two states to agree without changing either in the ghost model. This is a logical modeling device, not a runtime ability to predict crash outcomes. The authors report a Verus proof implementing the prophecy model over a natural model using prophecy variables. The PoWER-to-Crash-Hoare-logic proof in Rocq/Perennial is metalogical and trusts a translation of PoWER semantics, since PoWER was not implemented in Rocq. The Verus correspondence to crash invariants is entirely machine-checked within Verus. Formal theorem bodies are in artifacts; this reading examined paper explanations only. Crash states can be specified through rec(bytes), commonly allowing pre-operation or post-operation abstract state. Transition permissions instead authorize pairs of durable states. Blanket permissions cover arbitrary recovery-equivalent transitions; single-use permissions authorize a mutating transition once and are consumed or invalidated. A blanket permission can manufacture single-use permissions only for its allowed transitions. Initial recoverability and all permission constructions remain proof obligations. Tentative writes change only addresses irrelevant to rec and need no value-specific proof. Committing writes are a single aligned atomic chunk, typically after flushing tentative data, so only old/new durable states matter. Recovery writes rely on idempotent recovery that overwrites all possibly torn bytes on retry. In-place writes can use weaker specifications with many allowed outcomes, but the authors have no verified examples or helper-library support for that category. Atomic PoWER adds durable ghost resources owned by atomic invariants, proof callbacks and completion objects for consumed transition permissions. Completions witness an issued/applied operation even if another thread later changes its key. This extension needs concurrency facilities beyond the minimal core features; a tool-agnostic core does not imply arbitrary concurrent proofs in plain sequential Dafny. Concurrency allows multiple readers, or disjoint statically allocated storage regions with exclusive access during writes. It excludes read/write or write/write overlap within one region because callers must know its current logical state. Sharded wrappers establish linearizable individual create/read/update/delete/list operations, not cross-shard transactions. The reusable inner implementation still supplies a transactional API to wrappers. Corruption is modeled by a fixed device bitmask with at most c potentially faulty physical bits. A zero mask bit reads correctly; a marked bit can return either value independently on each read. The trusted CRC axiom distinguishes byte strings at Hamming distance 1 through c. Current ECMA CRC-64 implementation uses c=1 for arbitrary lengths; the cited c=3 for data shorter than about1 GiB is not exploited. Detection is conditional on that device-wide bound, not a guarantee against arbitrary bursts, malicious rewrites, rollback or unbounded media failure. Reader qualification: integrity proofs must cover corrupted data and checksum bytes, repeated/noncontiguous address mappings, and the chosen CDB codeword distance under the same physical-bit bound. The paper reports verified checking and a trusted CRC library; it does not derive an unrestricted cryptographic collision-resistance guarantee. Detecting a mismatch permits reporting corruption, not necessarily repairing damage or preserving availability. Tick-Tock’s old-checksum/new-data mismatch after a crash is not a small-bit corruption event relative to the old data. CRC(D0) can collide with CRC(D1-prime) even if D1-prime differs by only bounded media corruption from D1, because D0 versus D1-prime may differ arbitrarily. The paper gives a logical counterexample to the algorithm in its model, not an independently reproduced NOVA-Fortis artifact exploit. CDB stores one of two known eight-byte values CRC(0) and CRC(1), with aligned crash atomicity and sufficient corruption separation assumed/proved for the primitive. Two data/CRC slots accompany it. Write the inactive slot and checksum, flush, atomically switch CDB, flush. The selector identifies the committed slot independently of potentially matching stale checksums. This costs extra storage and flushes; it does not remove hardware atomicity assumptions. CapybaraKV values contain a fixed-size item and a list of fixed-size elements, with fixed-size keys. The abstract state has on-abort and on-commit maps. Ordinary operations affect the latter; abort restores it from the former; commit publishes it to the former. A crash during commit may commit or abort, while other uncommitted operations abort. Reads within a transaction see tentative operations, so visible results need not already be durable. Implementation uses main/item/list tables, per-field CRCs, validity CDBs, copy-on-write updates and a physical redo journal. Journal commit writes a CRC of pending entries then flips a CDB; replay installs operations and clears the journal. Volatile key index and free lists rebuild on startup. Correctness depends on recovery traversal, bounds, allocation and CRC checks, not merely the commit selector. Capacity is statically allocated at initialization with maximum key/item/list counts and sizes. No dynamic resizing, partial-value updates or range queries. All keys reside in a volatile Rust HashMap and must be indexed again at startup. Designed target is small records on tens of GiB of dedicated PM in a cloud-storage service. Prototype integration into an Azure Rust system is reported, not evidence of production deployment of all verified variants. Trusted pmcopy bridges Verus and compiler-generated representations. It requires repr(C) and derive(PmCopy), implements PmSafe/PmSized/Clone/PartialEq, generates specifications and static layout assertions checked by Rust. PmSafe includes numeric types, bool and char; composites require safe fields. Casts still require correct layout, valid discriminants/values and prior corruption checks. Compiler assertions caught a u128/i128 layout change; this is a concrete consistency check, not a proof of the macro or compiler. CapybaraNS stores a 64-bit logical timestamp and last hash. Advance increments and atomically persists them using CDB; Sign signs their binding. A trusted C# wrapper supplies CRCs, cryptography and serialization. This paper does not supply a complete distributed-notary protocol, a cryptographic implementation proof, remote attestation argument or availability theorem. Counter overflow handling and full security assumptions require the external specification. PM model permits independent eight-byte chunk reorderings until flush; backend write uses PMDK non-temporal stores or mov followed by clflushopt/clwb, and flush uses sfence. It deliberately overapproximates strongly ordered clflush and same-cache-line hardware ordering, including potential compiler reorderings. Eight-byte alignment/atomicity, backend calls and hardware behavior remain trusted. PoWER can use other models; current model is not a universal storage-device specification. Table 2 counts unverified pmcopy source but not its generated code. KV trusted count includes mock byte-vector PM plus Windows/Linux backends, concurrency and sharding wrappers. Trusted versus proved LOC therefore should not be interpreted as executable core size alone. Reported proof/code ratios are2.6 KV and2.4 NS; LOC is not a measure of specification adequacy. After that experience, porting the PM spec to Dafny took under an hour, porting helper lemmas about an hour, and implementing/verifying NS about nine hours after its spec and C# wrapper were already written. This is author experience, not a controlled productivity comparison. On Linux6.9.3 with i7-11850H eight physical cores and32 GB RAM, KV verifies in54s with one thread or23s with eight; NS takes12s with one. Appendix expects KV1–2min serial or15–40s parallel on other hardware. Paper gives no independent proof replay in this reading and no controlled comparison against alternative verification approaches. Performance setup is a two-socket32-core machine with128 GB RAM and one128 GB Optane DC PMM, Debian Trixie/Linux6.12.10. All KV runs use the sharded variant with one shard per thread. Redis client/server run together but retain communication overhead; RocksDB uses memory-mapped files and non-temporal log appends; Viper preallocates enough capacity except in utilization measurement. Append adds16 elements per record in random order; read-list returns the entire list; trim removes it. Other operations run once per record. Figure2 uses logarithmic latency axes and95% confidence intervals. KV matches or beats RocksDB but Viper is faster on several operations, including most writes; Redis is slowest. Windows/Azure20 GiB battery-backed DRAM tests run only KV, with up to2× improvement; other systems lack Windows support. YCSB uses15M keys,24-byte keys,1140-byte values and five executions per system. RunE range queries are omitted and RunA/RunB partial updates become full-value updates. X is uniform75% updates,5% read-modify-write and20% reads; Y/Z use50/50 or5/95 read/update with90% accesses to10% records. LoadE is omitted only from Figure4 as similar to LoadA. These modified workloads must not be called an unmodified full YCSB suite. At one thread KV is broadly comparable to Viper and often slightly slower. At16 threads it substantially leads Viper on update/read-heavy run phases but not every load phase; the broad prose claim of outperforming other systems needs this figure-level qualification. Viper is tested on one non-interleaved NVDIMM despite optimizations for interleaved PM. Authors attribute scaling issues partly to CCEH semaphore costs nearly doubling1→16 threads. This is reported profiling attribution, not isolated causal proof. Figure 4 read-heavy B/C/D scale better than write-heavy phases. Approximate 16-thread throughput is RunC 3.5 Mops/s, RunB/RunD 3.0, RunA 1.25, LoadA 0.4, RunF 1.1, RunX 0.9, RunY 1.2, RunZ 0.8 and LoadX 0.4. Values are visual estimates. Hash sharding distributes hot keys across shards, so this does not demonstrate performance under all accesses contending on one shard. Full-instance startup fills each store to its own out-of-space point with64-byte keys/1 KiB values; capacities and record counts can therefore differ. KV/Viper startup is seconds because volatile indexes rebuild, whereas RocksDB is milliseconds. Full Redis startup fails with memory allocation error. Table3 utilization instead uses YCSB LoadA and optimally provisions KV at18 GiB with no further growth. Comparing those startup/resource numbers requires keeping these distinct experiments separate. Artifact branch osdi25-artifact and Zenodo15306499 include implementations, scripts and proof guidance; CHL formalization lives in the Perennial repository rather than being bundled. Exact performance reproduction requires at least128 GB Optane, with128 GB DRAM/32 cores recommended; emulation can check workflow but changes performance. - SLTL standpoint model checking (2025)
    - title: Model Checking Linear Temporal Logic with Standpoint Modalities
    - what: Extends standpoint linear temporal logic (SLTL) with four history-information semantics in addition to step semantics: pure observation, public-history, decremental, and incremental. It supplies one history-DFA/model-checking construction that handles all five semantics, translates pure-observation SLTL to perfect-recall LTLK, and derives complexity bounds separating semantics and standpoint alternation depth. The formal semantics use separate finite transition systems Ta whose labels expose subsets Pa of propositions and define future-history satisfaction. Decremental nesting observes Pa intersections, while incremental nesting unions coalition observations; Example 3.5 gives explicit formulas and systems separating all five semantics. The algorithm computes bottom-up history DFAs using powerset constructions and products with subordinate DFAs, then applies standard LTL model checking. The paper proves PSPACE-completeness for full step/public SLTL and depth-1 pure-observation/decremental/incremental fragments, single-exponential time for step/public/decremental (and disjoint-observation pure observation), N-fold exponential time and (N-1)-EXPSPACE upper bound for incremental, and (d-1)-EXPSPACE membership for pure observation at alternation depth d.

No implementation or empirical benchmark is reported; the conclusion explicitly leaves experimental evaluation, stronger lower bounds, and analogous decremental space improvements as future work.

    - title: Data-Driven Verification of Procedural Programs with Integer Arrays
    - what: Introduces Tapis, a data-driven Horn-ICE decision-tree learner for procedural C-like programs with parametric-size integer/boolean arrays. The paper specifies finite-size array semantics (out-of-bounds reads return 0/false and writes have no effect), CHC encoding and Horn implications, then states the diagramization/lifting correctness results (proofs are deferred to the cited full version): Theorem 1 lifts a classifier of a consistent diagram sample; Theorem 2 guarantees consistency once each array has enough quantified indices. Attribute generation combines interval/octagon templates with patterns extracted from program assignments/guards. Bubble sort illustrates learned invariants; permutation preservation is explicitly outside that example. The implementation uses Clang frontend, C++ Tapis and Z3, tunes the teacher toward small arrays, and compares 215 programs: 121 SV-COMP array programs (84 safe, 37 unsafe) plus TAPIS-Bench (49 iterative, 37 recursive, 8 mutually recursive). Under 300-second runs on an 8-core 3.2GHz/16GB machine, Tapis solves 159/215 (95 safe iterative and 45 recursive safe plus 19 unsafe), versus Spacer 132 and Prophic3 118; it handles recursive procedures that several competitors cannot. Tapis uses at most two quantified variables per array/predicate in these sets and solves array-argmax for arbitrary N in 0.47 s where UAutomizer exceeds 36 minutes at N=5.

Contract variants are selected for supported contexts. §§2.3/4: Source C undefined behavior can compile into memory-safe bytecode. - Verifying an Efficient Algorithm for Computing Bernoulli Numbers (2025)
    - what: Isabelle/HOL verification and LLVM refinement of Harvey’s multimodular Bernoulli-number algorithm, including prime preparation, parallel modular numerator calculations, fast CRT reconstruction and denominator/sign recovery. Uses bounded machine arithmetic, Montgomery/table/reciprocal optimizations and specified GMP bindings. Exported code computes B_100000000 on a 128-thread cluster node in 45458 seconds; comparison with hand-optimized C++ is competitive for larger inputs under exploratory benchmark conditions. Tracks numerator residues instead of potentially undefined rational residues, all three modular cases, Kummer range reduction, nondeterministic refinement emptiness versus concrete LLVM, relaxed-accumulator bounds, 64-bit chunk table/reciprocal correction, certified prime-budget checks and sign-aware CRT. Preserves exact wrapper guarantees and external GMP/compiler/I/O boundaries, all benchmark table numbers, source inconsistencies and optimization-versus-mathematical proof effort.
    - limits: §2, pp.2–3: Bernoulli convention B1=−1/2; B0=1 and odd indices above 1 vanish. Even indices congruent 2 mod 4 are positive, multiples of 4 negative. Rational modular reduction requires denominator coprime to modulus. The denominator is the squarefree product of primes with p−1 dividing even k. The pre-existing AFP supplies Bernoulli foundations; Voronoi/Kummer congruences and concrete prime bounds were added for this development. §3, p.4: compute numerator N_k mod p for all odd primes, including denominator primes where B_k mod p is undefined. For p−1 dividing k, use −D_k/p mod p. Otherwise compute B_k mod p and multiply denominator factors modulo p. Fast sum requires 2^k≠1 mod p; slower fallback handles equality. Restricting to only fast primes lacks the required a priori coverage bound. Theorems 5–7, pp.3–4: Kummer gives range reduction using k prime=k mod (p−1), with k prime nonzero under the denominator exclusion, and factor k/k prime. Fast-sum theorem requires prime p≥5, 2≤k≤p−3 and primitive root g. It reindexes into m outer terms and n inner terms using the order of 2. These arithmetic assumptions differ from the later wrapper handling p=3 and larger original k. §3.1.1, p.5: nondeterminism-error monad refinement means implementation results belong to specification results and failure is controlled, but an abstract implementation with no results is still allowed. Refinement to LLVM later rules out an empty result set. The remainder-sum loop tracks power x^j, doubled residue 2^j s mod p and modular accumulator; explicit assertions expose bounds to later refinements. §3.1.2–3, pp.6–7: Montgomery state uses W=32, 64-bit accumulator and explicit nonoverflow arithmetic/casts. A relaxed accumulator is below (n+1)p and only needs final reduction. Refinement assumptions include a valid Montgomery context, n<2^W and correctly represented input. Export uses 32-bit modulus/inverse/value/residue parameters and 64-bit length/result; an interface width alone does not eliminate the stronger length proof condition. §3.2, pp.7–8: w=w prime=8 gives 64 binary digits per chunk and eight byte-indexed tables of 256 double-width words, 16 KiB total. Entries use relaxed Montgomery form so the hot loop mostly performs shifts, masks, indexed updates and additions. A precomputed floor(2^128/p) replaces division; a possible quotient error of one is corrected, requiring p<2^31. Remainder terms not divisible by 64 use the simpler loop. §3.3, p.9: final modular wrapper requires even nonzero k, odd prime 3≤p<2^31, denominator factor list, correct primitive root below p and correct order of 2. It creates the Montgomery inverse by Hensel lifting, applies range reduction or denominator-prime shortcut, multiplies denominator factors and converts out of Montgomery representation. The final result is exactly N_k mod p. §4.1–4.4, pp.10–12: an initial analytic bit-size bound and explicit prime-product inequality bound required sieve size. Reject if Y≥2^31; success is proved through k=105946388. Sieve produces odd primes and a smallest-prime-factor cache, denominator factors sharpen the bit budget, and fixed-point log bounds prune primes without floating point or huge integers. Tasks contain prime, primitive root, order and a placeholder residue. §4.4–4.5, p.12: primitive roots are found by testing candidates against prime factors of p−1; the factor cache also computes order. Parallel map preserves every task’s first three fields and fills the correct residue. t>1 is the map precondition, while the caller uses max(2,t). Parameters t,d affect parallel execution, not the mathematical result. This is shared-memory LLVM parallelism, not an asynchronous distributed protocol. §4.6, pp.12–13: special cases return 1,−1/2,0 for k=0,1,odd>1. General processing returns a success flag, numerator and denominator. Add N_k≡1 mod 2; all moduli are distinct primes and their product exceeds |N_k|. CRT returns residue num in [0,m); known sign gives N_k=num for positive indices and num−m for multiples of 4. This is not unsigned residue reconstruction without a sign theorem. §4.6.1–2, pp.13–14: fast CRT uses product/remainder trees, independent recursive branches and array refinement instead of explicit pointer trees. CRT and denominator product need arbitrary precision; GMP operations are imported through specified Hoare triples with an existence model. The model prevents contradictory specifications but does not prove GMP’s implementation correct. Replacing GMP with a verified library is discussed as independent work. §5, p.14: final wrapper Hoare triple assumes separate valid output memory locations, nonnegative signed 64-bit t,d and unsigned 32-bit k. It ensures valid GMP numerator/denominator outputs, k≤105946388 implies success, and every successful result equals the canonical numerator/denominator. A larger k is not guaranteed to fail; a successful larger case is still correct. Trust includes Isabelle, LLVM generator/compiler, separation-logic/model assumptions and specified GMP operations. §5/6, pp.14–15: generated C/C++ header and LLVM are used by a handwritten command-line driver. Timing callbacks instrument exported LLVM. Decimal conversion/file writing use an unverified GMP routine. Comparison also uses Ryzen 9 9900X single/12-core and Ryzen 7950X3D 16-core. Reported relative performance improves with k; cluster code is slightly faster over roughly 3e5–5e6, but authors explicitly deny a statistically rigorous comparison. No confidence intervals, run counts or repeatability protocol are given. §§7–8, pp.16–17: the cited O(k² log^(2+o(1)) k) complexity and practical-record history concern Harvey’s algorithm, not a newly mechanized cost theorem in this paper. A later subquadratic prime-power algorithm lacks an implementation according to the authors at publication. The development totals 32578 LOC; about 6 kLOC/20% is mathematical core. No artifact build or independent benchmark replay was performed.

    - what: Lean 4 certificate checker for positive, function-free Datalog conclusions. Formalizes least-model and proof-tree semantics and their equivalence; verifies computable ground-rule matching and tree/DAG validation. Offers unordered hash-map graphs with verified DFS acyclicity/local checks and ordered arrays with backward-index references. Adds preliminary safe-rule model checking; evaluates certificates converted from Nemo traces. Separates checking individual derivations from checking closure/model completeness. Gives partial-substitution matching equivalence under inhabited constants, ordered-body indexing, a reusable DFS correctness invariant based on reachability from cycles rather than cycle membership, and compact topologically ordered proof graphs. Benchmarks show sharing can greatly reduce tree certificates, while explicit input facts are absent from the prototype JSON and must be treated as leaf assumptions.

Grounding maps every variable to a constant; computable matching uses partial substitutions. grounding_substitution_equiv explicitly requires Inhabited constants so unmatched variables can receive a default. Atom/relation comparisons and hash-based executable representations require suitable equality/hash instances. Tree validity uses ordered children exactly matching the grounded rule-body list, or a database leaf; empty-body rules can also justify leaves. It proves a supplied derivation of a fact, not completeness of a reasoner or all facts being listed. Program indexing by head/body relation sequence must contain the correct source rules. Unordered graph is complete as a data structure: every predecessor is a vertex key. Acyclicity plus locally valid nodes yields a proof tree for every vertex. This completeness means no dangling graph references, not completeness of logical consequences. All vertices checked, not merely one selected root. HashMap/HashSet DFS distinguishes current walk for cycles from fully verified nodes for sharing. Theorem9 is scoped to calls from the driver and valid verified-node invariant; no unrestricted correctness claim for arbitrary bogus cached sets/walks. Ordered arrays require each predecessor index strictly less than current index and validate local rule steps. §5 model check requires safe rules (head variables also appear in body). It checks all matching body substitutions against a finite candidate interpretation, with partial ground rule activeness invariant. This is unoptimized preliminary functionality, not the procedure whose scalability Table 1 establishes. Prototype JSON does not explicitly encode original database facts; every no-predecessor node is treated as an assumed fact. Thus validation is relative to those supplied leaf assumptions. It cannot catch an invented leaf unless original database membership is separately supplied/checked. Authors explicitly call for explicit facts for production. Input fact/rule ingestion from original sources such as CSV is outside certification scope. Lean kernel theorem checking and compiled standalone execution are distinct trust paths; paper does not verify Lean compiler/runtime. Certificate soundness for selected facts is not complete materialization correctness. - A Generalised Union of Rely–Guarantee and Separation Logic Using Permission Algebras (2024)
    - what: GenRGSep is an Isabelle/HOL library generalizing rely-guarantee separation logic to resource models without guaranteed units or cancellativity. It supplies permission/multi-unit/single-unit algebra classes,compositional resource constructions,a generic relational-action concurrent language,explicit stabilization operators,and a reported mechanized operational soundness theorem. Identifies why Vafeiadis-style operational safety nearly extends to noncancellative resources but needs stronger preservation of local state on silent framed steps when external choice retains its surrounding command. Conjunction still needs all local resources cancellative. Distinguishes a weaker atomic framing condition from requiring the atomic relation to admit the corresponding unframed transition. Paper’s result concerns the generic logic/library,not a production implementation.
    - limits: Permission algebra requires partial commutativity/associativity,compatibility laws and positivity;it need not have units or cancellation. Multi-unit and single-unit classes add those respective structures. Total HOL addition is only constrained by algebra laws on compatible resources;behavior on incompatible sums cannot silently be used as valid resource composition. Proof system works over local/shared state pairs and relational atomic actions. Environment rely relation constrains shared changes;guarantee constrains observable updates. Local state splits under parallel composition while shared state remains common. Instantiating a real language requires sound resource and atomic-action models beyond this generic framework. Theorem2 says a derivable triple and its precondition imply safe n for every finite n. safe enforces postcondition only when command is skip,checks rely/program/framed steps,and records observable guarantee updates. It does not prove termination,fairness,progress,deadlock freedom or network-fault tolerance. Conjunction rule retains a global side condition:every possible local state must be cancellative. Removing cancellation from the base algebra does not make all standard conjunction reasoning available over arbitrary noncancellative instances. Silent τ transitions must preserve the same unframed local resource in the strengthened frame-safety clause. This is essential to the external-choice proof;allowing merely some decomposed residual resource is insufficient. Observable updates generate guarantee obligations without forcing guarantee reflexivity for silent actions. Predicates are shallow HOL functions;rely/guarantee,stabilization and atomic proof obligations are supplied mathematical relations/predicates. - A Verified Earley Parser (2024)
    - what: Isabelle/HOL formalization of an inductive Earley recognizer, refinement through a bin-wise fixed-point algorithm to executable functional lists, and a pointer-guided parser producing one parse tree. Recognizer correctness and successful parse-tree existence equivalence require terminal-only input and an epsilon-free grammar. Returned-tree soundness and a termination argument are proved for generated pointer structures. Explains why one-pass list-bin processing misses completion opportunities for epsilon rules and retains an explicit epsilon-free premise. Separates item equality, refinement, pointer invariants, single-tree soundness and tree-existence equivalence from enumeration of all parses. Uses first reduction-pointer monotonicity to terminate even for cyclic grammars; gives informal O(n^4) time and O(n^3) pointer-space estimates, rather than attributing optimal Earley bounds to this implementation.
    - limits: Grammar is a finite rule list plus start symbol over a common symbol type. Nonterminals are all rule LHS symbols plus the start symbol; terminals are the remaining symbols. is_word G omega excludes nonterminals from the input. Abstract item completeness and correctness explicitly assume is_word. The inductive Earley specification supports epsilon rules, but executable Earley_eq_Earley_L, correctness_recognizer and correctness_build_tree_Earley_L require epsilon_free G: every RHS is nonempty. Lifting this restriction is future work. No verified epsilon-elimination preprocessing is delivered here. Each bin contains distinct items with end index equal to bin index. List insertion appends new items and merges reduction pointers into existing entries. Termination of bin processing relies on well-formed bounded items and finite candidate counts, not arbitrary malformed bin arguments. build_tree_prime termination requires wf_tree_input: sound_ptrs, mono_red_ptr, valid bin/input indices and valid entry index. Pointer soundness includes earlier origin bins for reductions, bounds and operation semantics. Only the FIRST reduction triple is required to have a strictly earlier reduction entry within the current bin. wf_item_yield_build_tree_prime additionally assumes wf_bins. Returned-tree corollary assumes epsilon_free and successful build_tree over Earley_L-generated bins, and proves rule-tree well-formedness, start root and full input yield. Existential successful tree iff derivation additionally assumes is_word. The algorithm extracts one parse tree, not a forest enumerating every ambiguous or cyclic derivation. Nevertheless the final theorem DOES establish existence of a returned tree iff a valid derivation exists under its premises. The phrase no completeness for trees concerns all possible trees, not failure to recognize some valid word. Partial functions in HOL use domain-theoretic definitions; termination is proved on stated valid inputs. Option None representing undefinedness is not a runtime detector that can return after discovering an infinite computation. Arbitrary externally supplied pointer cycles are outside the proved termination domain. Complexity is explicitly informal with fixed grammar: rule count and maximum RHS size are constants. More than 6,000 formalization lines are reported, but no formal complexity theorem or proof-effort breakdown is supplied. Scala extraction and execution do not constitute a verified compiler/runtime chain. Evaluation measures the exported recognizer, not a full byte-level lexer or full parse-tree production pipeline. Five toy grammars, unary inputs a^n and ten-run means do not establish representative production workload performance. Hardware, Scala/JVM versions, exact source dataset, variance and raw timings are not supplied in §7. Imperative cached refinement, grammar indexing, next-symbol grouping and epsilon support remain future work. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed-system implementation or LLM agent is evaluated.

- Confidence-based neural 2-safety (2024)
    - title: Verifying Global Two-Safety Properties in Neural Networks with Confidence
    - what: Defines confidence-based global 2-safety properties unifying robustness and fairness, and verifies them by self-composing a DNN and replacing softmax with a sound piecewise-linear over-approximation checked by Marabou. The property compares every sufficiently close input pair when at least one output has confidence above a threshold, allowing class changes near low-confidence decision boundaries while requiring high-confidence predictions to agree. The paper proves soundness and bounds softmax approximation error, gives a complete Marabou-based counterexample procedure for the approximated network, and uses binary search to synthesize minimum robust/fair confidence. Experiments cover German Credit, Adult, Law School and COMPAS models with global robustness and sensitive-attribute fairness queries.

Marabou completeness removes solver false positives, but abstraction can produce spurious counterexamples. High confidence as a precondition can make poorly calibrated networks vacuously safe; current method handles roughly two to five outputs and does not establish training-data generalization.

    - what: PotPie compiles an embedded source program, its Hoare proof and its specification into a related target language, preserving a selected partial specification even when the program compiler changes other behavior. Gives a correct-by-construction CC workflow and a Tree workflow with an untrusted certificate generator or a less-assured boolean checker. Coq formalization proves conditional soundness; toy examples include deliberate miscompilation. Makes specification meaning preservation explicit via state correspondence and bidirectional assertion semantics, separately from target proof validity. Uses a manually translated implication database for consequence rules and structural compiler equations to transport other Hoare rules. Details source/target well-formedness, stack-purity obligations, certificate-versus-boolean trust, localized UIP axioms and partial-correctness/termination boundaries.

They are embedded semantics, not C/Rust/assembly or machine-word execution. Practical lower-level logics, pointers, optimizing control-flow passes and scalability are future work. Partial correctness of a selected postcondition does not establish full behavioral equivalence, termination or any property omitted from that specification. Helper multiplication/exponentiation need separate termination proofs, and target termination is reproved rather than automatically transported. No total correctness of the approximation algorithms is established by their Hoare triples. Definition3 requires pre/postcondition meaning equivalence on source stores and target stacks related by the chosen bijective variable mapping. Compiling both assertions toFalse could yield a valid target Hoare triple without preserving intended meaning. CC requires specification soundness; Tree certificate validity alone does not supply it. Users manually translate a valid source implication database and prove corresponding target implications. These finite assertions can be preserved even if the whole compiler is incorrect. Automatic generation of these obligations via weakest preconditions is proposed but not implemented. CC needs structural equations for assignment/substitution, skip, sequence, if and while, plus source well-formedness and stack-preserving compiled expressions/functions. Thus arbitrary semantics-preserving control-flow transformations do not automatically qualify. Completeness language is conditional on the stated proof obligations and supported structure. Stack expressions in assignments and branch/loop tests must preserve the stack. Function-call effects/arity/stack shape require proofs. Source functions are mutation-free outside locals and immutable parameters, while target calls can access the whole stack. Definition1 constrains mapped variables/parameters but leaves extra stack suffix unconstrained. CC trust includes Coq kernel, mechanized semantics/Hoare definitions and two localized UIP axioms for assertion and function-environment types. It does not assume universal UIP. Opaque CC proof terms may retain dependency on source semantics. Tree certificate path constructs stk_valid_tree, whose Coq checking plus valid_tree_can_construct_hl_stk gives a target Hoare proof without UIP. OCaml certificate generation is untrusted for accepted checked certificates. Boolean fallback adds an unverified OCaml checker to the trust base and is not formal correctness evidence. Certificate generation can fail on mutually recursive functions or malformed trees. A boolean fallback for modular stack-purity checks does not repair this certificate limitation. Target specification preservation still needs its own user proof even if a certificate typechecks. Square-root example’s printed formal postcondition is a pair of cross-multiplied natural-number inequalities under preconditionTrue. Interpreting it as rational approximation additionally requires nonzero relevant denominators (b,y,epsilon denominator); these are not in the displayed precondition. The mathematical reading must not silently replace the stated encoded relation.

- distributional probabilistic model checking (2024)
    - what: Extends probabilistic model checking from expected rewards to full reward distributions for DTMCs and MDPs, supporting variance, quantiles, value-at-risk and CVaR for rewards accumulated until co-safe LTL goals. The paper defines categorical and quantile distribution representations, distributional queries and optimization semantics, and reduces co-safe LTL goals to reachability with a DFA product. Algorithm 1 computes a DTMC distribution by forward propagation while separating non-target BSCCs that yield infinite reward, with a provable per-atom error bound and truncation mass ε. Risk-neutral distributional value iteration (DVI) chooses actions by expected value; risk-sensitive DVI uses the CVaR dual slack variable, a discretized product MDP and a convergence result whose error is O(stride). A PRISM prototype evaluates betting, Deep Sea Treasure, obstacle, UAV and energy models, with risk-sensitive products up to 2.3e6 states and runtime up to 15,051 s; distributions converge toward ground truth as atom counts increase. DTMC forward computation is often faster than DVI on large PRISM benchmarks, but DVI can be faster when Vmax is high.

    - title: Formal Verification of the Empty Hexagon Number
    - what: Formalizes in Lean the geometric-to-SAT reduction behind h(6)=30: every set of 30 planar points in general position contains an empty convex hexagon. The development defines convexity/emptiness in mathlib, proves a triangle characterization, reduces geometry to triple-orientation Boolean assignments, proves canonical-position symmetry breaking, and verifies the optimized Heule–Scheucher CNF encoding. A distributed CaDiCaL/cake_lpr computation supplies the n=30 unsatisfiability certificate. Sections 3–4 connect Lean convex-hull predicates to triangle emptiness and determinant-based orientations; σPtInTriangle_iff under four-point general position closes an implicit gap in prior work, and OrientationProperty proves that holes depend only on triple orientations. Section 5 constructs a six-step canonical-position transformation (rotation, translation, projective map, sorting, reflection and return from infinity) and proves existence of a σ-equivalent canonical set. Section 6 defines orientation, triangle, cap/cup and hole variables plus 16 clause families; variable-defining and orientation clauses are proved, while forbidden configurations imply six-holes. The n=30 CNF is partitioned into 312,418 subproblems, solved by CaDiCaL 1.9.5 with LRAT proofs checked on the fly by cake_lpr in 25,876.5 CPU hours (~3 CPU years). The Lean encoder emits CNF below 1 s on a laptop; a comparison g(6) corollary takes 28 s to solve versus Marić's 787 s and uses O(n⁴) rather than O(n⁶) clauses. The formalization required ~300 hours/3 months and ~4.7k Lean lines, and corrected an orientation-map error and a lex-order/code mismatch in prior work.

- Extended Threshold Automata (2024)
    - title: Parameterized Verification of Round-Based Distributed Algorithms via Extended Threshold Automata.
    - what: Extends threshold automata (TA) with shared-variable increments, decrements, and resets, including cycles, and develops parameterized coverability and reachability checking. Threshold values are interval-abstracted into abstract counter systems (ACS); a well-structured transition-system backward algorithm computes predecessor bases, builds an error graph, and uses SMT constraints to reject spurious abstract counterexamples. A (0,1)-abstraction handles reachability. Soundness and completeness hold for the abstractions; termination requires restricted updates, while the general extension is a semi-decision procedure. The concrete TA model includes process-location counters, shared variables, parameter vectors and linear resilience conditions. Algorithm 1 computes upward-closed predecessor bases and retains visited transitions so all paths can be checked for non-spuriousness; Lemma 5 gives completeness and Corollary 2 soundness. Theorem 1 proves termination when all update vectors are nonnegative and no resets occur. PRA uses symbolic BDDs; examples include reliable broadcast, Byzantine/crash consensus, commit, phase king and multi-round Red Belly Blockchain. The reachability abstraction preserves only location occupancy and is exact for reachability/coverability specifications.

Safety properties are agreement, validity and unforgeability; liveness and communication timing are outside the evaluated model. - ForEx hyperliveness verification (2024)
    - title: Automated Software Verification of Hyperliveness.
    - what: Introduces Forall-Exist Hoare Logic (FEHL) and ForEx, a constraint-based verifier for finite-program ∀k∃l relational properties (Forall-Exist Hoare Tuples). The method symbolically postpones existential nondeterministic choices as parameters, computes parametric strongest postconditions, and discharges resulting first-order constraints with SMT. FEHL provides self-composition, sequencing, conditionals, loops and consequence rules; the paper proves soundness and completeness relative to sound/complete unary Hoare and under-approximate systems. ForEx implements eager restriction satisfiability checks, a minimal C-like language with arrays/bitvectors, Z3 support for linear integer arithmetic, arrays and finite bitvectors, and guess-and-check invariant generation. Experiments compare ForEx against HyPA, PCSat and HyPro on k-safety, GNI, refinement and related benchmarks. ForEx is faster on solved instances but its counting-based loop alignment misses context-dependent alignments and it cannot prove termination of existential loops, leaving some GNI instances unsolved.

    - title: Using Four-Valued Signal Temporal Logic for Incremental Verification of Hybrid Systems
    - what: Defines a four-valued STL semantics and an incremental verification algorithm that runs alongside set-based reachability. One unknown value denotes set-based ambiguity and a second denotes missing future reachability information, enabling early termination when a verdict is conclusive. The paper constructs Boolean until over minimal unitary decompositions, lifts operators to three- and four-valued signals via under/overapproximations, and proves refinement theorems connecting reachable-set verdicts to every covered execution. Algorithm 1 updates atomic predicates per newly computed interval and propagates signals; irrelevant prefixes are discarded. A branch refinement strategy splits reachability by discrete transitions or initial-state regions when one set mixes divergent behaviors. Evaluation covers bouncing-ball formulas (including inaccurate-set unknowns), a CommonRoad lane-change trajectory, and a nine-dimensional genetic oscillator.

    - what: Introduces Hitchhiking, a massively parallel on-the-fly LTL emptiness algorithm for GPUs. Hitchhiking adapts the Map accepting-predecessor algorithm to exploration-time GPU execution. It maintains open, active, and interrupted sets plus a monotone maximal-predecessor function; detailed lemmas establish finite rounds, propagation invariants, cycle detection, and no-cycle termination, and a thread-safety argument explains atomic maxima and barriers. GPUexplore 3.0 integrates the algorithm with a compressed tree hash table, work claiming, generated CUDA successor functions, and Spot NBA construction. The evaluation compares Hitchhiking with Map, Spin NDFS, and 1/32-core LTSmin over 96 BEEM instances spanning 150,000–1.2 billion states.

    - what: Reports a Lean 4 formalization of soundness, completeness and the finite model property for coalition logic with individual/common knowledge. Main contribution is mechanized logical metatheory and proof engineering, not an implemented distributed-system case study. Records exact semantic/frame assumptions, positive-length common-knowledge paths, canonical effectivity cases, closure changes needed for deep embedding, finite-state construction, staged Set/Finset/List proofs and the concrete N-maximality derivation.
