    - number: Table 2 broadcast properties: 5.61, 6.87, 27.64, 6.75 s
    - number: simplified-consensus properties: 4.13–4.68 s
    - number: complete compositional verification <70 s
    - limits: Fixed n sequential processes communicate through reliable fully connected asynchronous point-to-point links; delays are finite but unbounded, steps interleave, each receive is atomic and sender identities distinguish quorum members. Up to t<n/3 are Byzantine; f≤t is the actual fault count. The threshold abstraction assumes faulty senders cannot impersonate arbitrarily many distinct processes. Communication closure is essential: each process uses only messages for its current round, discards earlier tags and buffers later tags. Monotone send counters and threshold guards admit the prior ByMC reduction. Guarantees do not automatically extend to arbitrary protocols with cross-round data dependencies, timing constraints or changing membership. Reliable communication is encoded by progress assumptions on enabled rules and source-location emptiness. This excludes scheduler executions that indefinitely withhold enabled productive actions. Added consensus fairness is different: some round r has every correct process first deliver r mod2 in that round’s binary-value broadcast. Neither fairness follows from asynchronous reliability alone. Algorithm1 is the DBFT variant without coordinator/timeouts. The second DBFT variant uses partial synchrony, but this paper replaces that mechanism with a good-round assumption. It does not prove a synchronizer, coordinator rotation, timeout correctness or that the deployed environment enforces the assumption. Threshold models describe correct processes and abstract Byzantine influence with f-offset guards; global send counters abstract possible local receipt histories. Parameterized checking ranges over symbolic parameters satisfying n>3t≥3f, rather than testing a list of network sizes. Soundness still depends on faithful manual abstraction and ByMC’s reductions/SMT checks. Inner broadcast verification establishes justification,obligation,uniformity and termination. Replacement must preserve all behaviors relevant to the outer consumer because contestants is shared and the outer algorithm can proceed before the broadcast finishes. The paper argues this and supplies encoded preconditions; it is not a machine-checked source-to-source refinement of production code. ByMC handles a restricted LTL fragment and one-round systems. Cross-superround agreement,initial validity and existential good-round termination require manually chosen intermediate formulas and mathematical composition arguments. The model checker does not directly discharge each final quantified formula as written. The proof covers binary agreement,validity and eventual decision for the displayed algorithm. It does not prove blockchain transaction semantics,multi-value reduction,ledger consistency across all block heights,network/cryptographic code,resource bounds or end-to-end behavior of the deployed Red Belly software. Processes continue participating after deciding so others can finish; only the first decision matters. Text states safe exit after two later rounds but does not supply a verified executable stopping implementation. A process that halts immediately on first decision would change progress assumptions.

- Refinement of Parallel Algorithms down to LLVM (2022)
    - what: Adds parallel execution to the Isabelle Refinement Framework and generates verified LLVM. A state-nondeterminism-error monad reports reads, writes, allocation and frees; parallel composition assumes feasible allocation pairs and fails on races. Concurrent separation logic and a VCG prove low-level commands; Sepref refines pure list algorithms to in-place arrays, tracks pointer equalities and splits arrays for disjoint parallel updates. A parallel introsort/pdqsort-style algorithm is proved total-correct and benchmarked against C++. The memory model uses never-reused blocks, so use-after-free and allocation conflicts are detectable. The M-monad invariant requires consistency and an execution avoiding every finite forbidden block set. The disjoint concurrency rule composes Hoare triples; with_split and npar refine independent list subcomputations to same-array disjoint slices. Parallel psort partitions, falls back when depth/size is small or partition is unbalanced, and uses median-of-64 sampling. The final theorem states in-place return of the original pointer and sorted-permutation contents. Generated LLVM is instantiated for uint64 and strings. Figure 2 compares verified, std::sort(par-unseq), and Boost sample_sort over many distributions on laptop/server; Figure 3 shows speedup versus core count. Results are comparable on laptop integers, slower for server strings and highly parallel speedup. The semantics and generated LLVM text remain within an explicit trust boundary: Isabelle’s kernel, the shallow LLVM embedding and the code generator are trusted, and parallel execution uses an external C++ TBB primitive.

The framework targets a small LLVM fragment, multicore CPUs and a parallel combinator; locks, atomics, read-only fractional ownership and GPUs are future work. Sorting correctness assumes a weak ordering and array length represented by a fixed-width word; code generation fixes widths to 64 bits and uses an int64 size signature. Benchmark evidence is runtime comparison, not a proof of speed or broad hardware scalability; no distributed network model, Rust/Verus, TLA+ or LLM agent is evaluated. The trusted code base includes Isabelle’s inference kernel, the shallow embedding of a small LLVM fragment and the text code generator. The parallel primitive calls an external C++ implementation using tbb::parallel_invoke. Correctness is proved against the embedded semantics; the paper does not prove the LLVM compiler, TBB runtime or complete LLVM-to-binary toolchain correct.

Physical equivalence matches all per-cycle output sequences and relates reset final circuit to resulting spec state. §4.5: PE maps arbitrary wire traffic to some sequence of legal spec operations.     - what: Isabelle/HOL correctness proof of a BKR-style univariate real-arithmetic decision procedure with rational-coefficient polynomial atoms.     - title: Brief Announcement: Automating and Mechanising Cutoff Proofs for Parameterized Verification of Distributed Protocols
    - what: Presents a framework that derives and mechanizes simulation-based cutoff proofs from a cutoff instance, node mapping and action translation, reducing unbounded safety verification to finite checking plus first-order satisfiability. Protocols are asynchronous RML relation systems with nondeterministic atomic actions. For large instance L and cutoff C, sim maps each large node to a cutoff node; Ω filters state components relevant to first violation and τ translates each large action to zero or more cutoff actions, allowing stuttering. The simulation relation requires Ω(σL(N))⊆σC(sim(N)); its inductiveness is encoded as FOL formula (1), while violation preservation is formula (2). Theorem 1 states that UNSAT of both formulas plus a safe cutoff implies all instances safe. The ring leader-election example uses a two-node cutoff for two elected leaders.
    - number: two-node leader-election cutoff
    - number: FOL formulas (1) and (2)
    - number: Z3 backend
    - number: few-second prototype checks
    - limits: The protocol is modeled in RML with asynchronous message passing, atomic nondeterministic actions and a safety property; the designer must supply protocol, cutoff, sim, Ω and τ. The method checks first violations and requires a sound FOL encoding/SMT result. Cutoff synthesis is future work, and the implementation was still work-in-progress; no completeness claim for arbitrary protocols or liveness properties is made.

- Bridging arrays and ADTs in recursive proofs (2021)
    - what: Presents a fully automatic method for synthesizing recursively defined relational invariants that prove equivalence of paired object implementations when one uses arrays and the other algebraic data types (ADTs). The method encodes initialization, paired transitions, applicability and output equality as CHCs; Algorithm 1 builds a recursive invariant schema, Algorithm 2/3 bridge producer/consumer operations for linear scans, and Algorithm 4/5 use noop observations for sets/maps. Candidate relations are validated by structural induction with AdtInd/Z3. The paper formalizes equivalence as an inductive invariant over a composition of two deterministic objects, with initialization, consecution for every paired operation, precondition applicability in both directions, and output equality. It defines producer/consumer/noop classifications via a partial ordering on ADT states and synthesizes a Skolem-like updated array state plus matching constraints. Recipe 1 handles stacks/queues with an index and can infer loop invariants; Recipe 2 handles sets, multisets and maps by updating only the observed array cell while preserving all other inputs. Validation is structural induction rather than recursion-free SMT checking, and user lemmas are optional (one multiset lemma was needed in evaluation).
    - number: 10 benchmark variants in Table 1
    - number: stack 2.81 s and queue 40.61–42.18 s
    - number: set 2.12/19.24 s; multiset 32.62/3.59 s; map 1.95/5.83 s
    - number: MacBook Pro 2 GHz Intel Core i5, 8 GB RAM
    - limits: Objects are modeled syntactically as predicates obtained from symbolic execution; loop effects must already be expressed as quantified formulas. Programs are deterministic and each enabled precondition has a successor/output. The approach targets finite sets of operations and list-shaped ADTs; it assumes suitable classifications/recipes and SMT quantifier-elimination/array reasoning. CHC solving is undecidable in general, proof search can dominate runtime, and the evaluation is textbook data structures rather than large real software. The method requires monotonic/structural-induction support in AdtInd and may need user lemmas for harder cases.

- CoMuS hierarchical modular verification (2021)
    - title: Modular Verification of Concurrent Programs via Sequential Model Checking
    - what: Introduces CoMuS, a fully automatic reduction of safety verification for a fixed number of concurrent threads to sequential model-checking tasks, with lazy environment learning and a hierarchy-aware verification order. The main-thread program inserts env_move at interleaving cut-points and initially havocs environment-written shared variables. Counterexample paths induce ReachE(alpha,beta) queries; infeasible queries generalize alpha/beta and refine env_move, while feasible queries produce promises of error that become assertions and may expose environment locals or pcE as new variables. Environment queries are answered by a sequential environment program using try_start to model reachable non-initial computations. The algorithm maintains an overapproximation invariant, is sound for Safe and Real Violation outcomes, and makes progress by shrinking represented environment transitions or expanding states known to lead to errors. It is guaranteed to terminate for finite variable domains but not generally for infinite domains.
    - number: CoMuS was compared with Threader, VVT, and UL-CSeq using SeaHorn/CPAChecker backends on Ubuntu 16.04, 8GB RAM, with 3600-second timeouts for dynamic-program benchmarks and 1200 seconds for fib-bench. In chain-structured dynamic programs CoMuS scaled best as thread count increased; all tools failed on ring instances with at least four threads while CoMuS verified all tested chain instances. On the general benchmark subset CoMuS was typically outperformed.
    - limits: Semantics is sequentially consistent interleaving with a fixed number of threads; synchronization is modeled atomically. Safety assertions are placed in the main thread, and cut-point/interleaving reduction must preserve safety. The prototype supports only a C subset, lacks alias analysis and dynamic thread creation, and depends on the sequential checker (SeaHorn) for infinite-state capabilities. Termination is not guaranteed over infinite domains; hierarchy-sensitive performance degrades on rings/general programs.

- DSS (2021)
    - title: Detectable Sequential Specifications for Recoverable Shared Objects
    - what: Defines detectability by transforming an ordinary sequential object specification into a detectable sequential specification (DSS). Per-process abstract state remembers a prepared operation and its response. prep-op announces the operation, exec-op performs it, and resolve reports whether it took effect and its response; ordinary operations remain available without detection. Section 2 gives the state transformation and four operation axioms. prep-op and resolve are total and idempotent, while exec-op requires the matching prepared operation with no recorded response. An auxiliary parity bit can distinguish repeated identical operations. DSS is combined with a separate concurrency correctness condition and leaves nesting recovery to the application. Section 3 derives a queue from the Michael–Scott/durable queue: tagged per-thread pointers record operation preparation and completion, CAS and helping maintain the linked list, and Appendix A supplies a centralized recovery scan. A variation replaces centralized recovery with individual recovery. Theorem 1 states lock-freedom and strict linearizability, but the article omits the analysis and detailed model. Section 4 measures failure-free queue throughput on real Optane memory.
    - number: up to 20 threads on 20 cores
    - number: 30-second runs, ten runs per point, standard deviation <2% of mean
    - number: non-detectable DSS nearly 3× detectable DSS throughput at low parallelism
    - number: MS up to 1.5× non-detectable DSS at two threads
    - limits: A recovering process must retain its identifier across crashes to query its previous operation; this conflicts with the fresh-identifier model underlying durable linearizability. DSS specifies sequential behavior and requires a separate concurrent correctness condition. The queue uses asynchronous shared memory, persistent memory, volatile caches, explicit flushes and system-wide crashes. Correct nesting is an application responsibility. The correctness theorem is stated rather than proved in this article. Experiments cover failure-free runs, use debug compilation at O0 and sequentially consistent atomics, and do not measure crash recovery latency. The log queue comparator is the authors’ implementation and could be optimized further.

- dtree variable-length state storage (2021)
    - title: Recursive Variable-Length State Compression for Multi-Core Software Model Checking
    - what: Introduces dtree, a concurrent chain-of-balanced-trees storage structure for variable-length model-checker states, supporting partial reconstruction and incremental delta updates; integrates it into the DMC multi-core checker. The paper contrasts dtree with TreeDBS and Compact Tree, explains why fixed alignment fails under dynamic allocation, and defines a StateID combining root index and length. Its API supports insert, delta, full/partial get and nested sub-states, enabling models to update heap regions without reconstructing complete states. Dtree experiments model Michael-Scott queues, sorted linked lists and concurrent hash maps, then compare 118 BEEM fixed-length models against LTSmin/TreeDBS, Compact Tree and SPIN Collapse. Results expose the trade-off: dtree wins on variable-length variance but loses compression on fixed-length vectors because its chain can be less balanced.
    - number: up to 2.9x faster and 29% less memory for variable-length models
    - number: 118 BEEM models
    - number: 64 threads; 96 physical cores
    - number: Compact Tree up to 2.3x more compression
    - limits: State slots are 32-bit and StateID allocates a fixed 40-bit index plus length budget; the chain-of-trees shape trades fixed-length compression for append/dynamic allocation. TreeDBS/Compact Tree comparisons require padding or auxiliary storage and exclude models with unsupported adjacent −1 values or excessive size. DMC's search core is simple parallel BFS; experiments use 64 threads on one 96-core machine, so results are implementation- and workload-dependent. Future work includes better root tables and work stealing.

    - title: An Algebraic Method to Fidelity-based Model Checking over Quantum Markov Chains
    - what: Defines QCTL, a fidelity-based quantum analogue of CTL over super-operator-weighted quantum Markov chains, and decides formulas by synthesizing path super-operators and reducing fidelity threshold queries to existential-real quantifier elimination. - Ghost Signals: Verifying Termination of Busy Waiting (2021)
    - what: Develops a modular Hoare/separation-logic approach to termination of busy-waiting programs under fair scheduling. Ghost signals represent conditions other threads must establish; linear obligations require setting them. A well-founded partial order forbids waiting on a signal at or above any obligation held by the waiter. Data-structure invariants tie signals to real conditions, allowing resource-local proof of waiting over arbitrary shared structures. §2 derives the logic through thread-safe physical signals, non-thread-safe signals guarded by mutexes, arbitrary heap cells, then erasure into ghost state. An augmented operational semantics makes a thread get stuck if it exits with outstanding obligations; fork transfers obligations rather than discarding them. A program-order graph tracks the path carrying each obligation. A minimal infinitely-waited signal would have an infinite obligation path that can wait only on finitely-waited lower signals, yielding contradiction under fairness. Points-to/signal ownership prevents races. Finite-function equality/extensionality comes from the finite representation, not an assumed axiom for arbitrary Coq functions. §2, pp.3–7: auxiliary-peg selector is symmetric but guaranteed different from both pegs only for at least three pegs. This is a discrete sequential graph, with no simultaneous moves. §2, pp.6–7: regular relation allows every distinct pair; linear relation allows consecutive ordinal pegs; star relation requires distinct pegs and at least one equal zero, so zero is center. Three-peg linear/star graphs are isomorphic after relabelling, not equal under the displayed labels (linear center 1 versus star center 0). Endpoint role matters for distances. §2–2.1, pp.5–8: transforms remove/add largest disks, split/merge size ranges, or restrict arbitrary disks/pegs. Projecting a legal path can produce identical adjacent states when a removed disk moves, so rm_rep deletes adjacent repetitions before applying the smaller-puzzle path theorem. It need not delete all repeated states or establish shortestness. §2.1, pp.7–8: distance is least length of a connecting path in a finite state graph; gpath combines path legality, endpoint and size equal to distance. Double induction on disks and path length handles the largest disk moving once, twice or returning. Uniqueness applies to these regular perfect endpoints, not all shortest paths in all variants. §3.1, p.10: in regular three-peg arbitrary-state transfer, a greedy largest-disk destination move may be suboptimal. Greedy is optimal if one endpoint is perfect; for two arbitrary endpoints compare one- and two-jump strategies for the largest disk whose location differs, leaving larger disks fixed. The paper describes these formalized results but does not print all algorithm/optimality proofs. §3.2, pp.10–11: for linear three pegs, greedy is optimal. Distinct adjacent perfect pegs have distance (3^n−1)/2; the two outer pegs have 3^n−1; identical endpoints have zero. Its recurrence contains (3^(n−m)−1)/2; doubled cost satisfies the star Frame–Stewart recurrence. §5, p.14: lower bound generalizes from two endpoints to l+1 configurations, with intermediate codomains alternating between pairs of outer pegs.     - what: The paper develops GoL, a process-calculus model for shared memory, locks, read-write locks, and later channels, with behavioural types that encode happens-before synchronization. Type soundness and progress connect processes to µ-calculus types; model checking these types detects data races, lock safety/liveness, and mixed channel/shared-memory errors. The migoinfer+ extractor and Godel2/mCRL2 backend form a static toolchain. Beyond the abstract, the authors define race and lock properties over GoL, prove subject reduction, process safety/data-race transfer, and conditional equivalence of type and process liveness for terminating, may-converging, and finite-branching programs.     - what: Presents TA2SMT, a direct BitVector/real-arithmetic SMT encoding of timed-automata networks for bounded model checking, preserving TACK’s MITL property encoding while removing the intermediate CLTLoc representation and adding semantic and implementation fixes.     - what: Presents VTV, an Agda checker whose kernel and first-order semantic soundness theorem are formally verified for TESC proof objects. - APKeep: Realtime Network Verification for Real Networks (2020)
    - what: APKeep incrementally checks a symbolic model of network forwarding, filtering and header rewriting. Its Port-Predicate Map separates logical functions and their applications, and maintains Boolean packet equivalence classes by splitting only for changed behavior and merging equal port sets. An informal inductive proof establishes a minimum partition for the basic immediate-merge algorithm; experiments measure update-plus-loop-check cost, partition sizes, memory, link-failure queries and synthetic NAT updates. Records the precise EC equivalence relation, rule priority/hit analysis, split/transfer/merge algorithm, rewrite closure, delayed merging and separate partition optimizations, invariant and policy traversal, vendor PBR case, all dataset and comparison tables, partial-run counting and synthesized workloads. Distinguishes the basic minimum-partition theorem from optimized execution and exposes printed formula/pseudocode/data inconsistencies without inferring implementation faults.
    - limits: §2.1: Every element sends each header to exactly one logical action port. Headers in an EC must select the same port at every element, even elements the header never reaches. This partition can be finer than physical device behavior or reachable paths. An element topology node is an application of a logical element; one ACL applied twice has two nodes but one shared model update. §2.1/§3.2/Appendix A: Disjoint ECs cover all headers. Minimum partition additionally requires equal port vectors to imply same EC. Appendix A uses informal induction over split/transfer/merge and rule updates; it is not machine checked and does not prove fidelity of parsers, Java code, device behavior or every invariant checker. §3.2/Algorithm 1: Rule hit subtracts higher-priority matches; identify only action changes, including default. Pseudocode uses strict priority comparisons and assumes a well-defined priority order. Rule deletion omitted; modification represented by delete plus insert. No detailed argument for atomic multi-device update semantics. §3.2/Algorithm 2: Split predicates on partial overlap; copy port sets, transfer changed part, merge equal port sets and propagate transferred-set D. BDDs encode arbitrary sets rather than header rectangles. Equality is model forwarding/action equality, not observational equivalence of stateful network executions. §3.4/Algorithm 3: Rewriting to constants existentially forgets overwritten bits then constrains new values. Maintain pre-to-post predicate table; recursively split images until rewrites are representable by current predicates. This closure can require additional splits beyond the simple port-vector partition. Appendix A does not explicitly extend its minimum-partition induction to rewrite closure. §3.4 Eq.(2), visually confirmed: printed existential quantification joins true/false cofactors with conjunction. Existential elimination mathematically requires disjunction. Treat as a printed formula error, not evidence that JDD implementation uses wrong operation. Algorithm 3 calls UpdateRW although prose calls this Algorithm 2; rewrite-table notation abbreviates rule association. §3.5: Delayed merging records candidates and merges only when predicate count exceeds 500 by default. The immediate-minimum theorem does not literally describe states between these merges. Forwarding and ACL partitions are updated separately; loop validation checks a nonempty conjunction of one predicate from each, avoiding cross-product false positives. Minimum per component does not imply a globally minimum joint partition. §3.3/Appendix B: Incremental delta forwarding graph uses transferred predicates; loop means revisiting a device without modification, blackhole means no forwarding rule. Intentional ACL denial is not this blackhole definition. Printed traversal remembers graph nodes; device-versus-element, topology applications, ingress reachability and rewrite-aware history are abstracted rather than fully formalized. Appendix B/Algorithms 4–5: Construct graph from ports holding D, with virtual default node. Traverse from updated element applications, carrying predicate intersections/history. Algorithm 5 line 4 passes undefined predicates after initializing pset; default-edge check precedes edge intersection, apparently allowing an empty-intersection edge to flag. These are presentation concerns; no executable bug reproduced. §3.3/§5.1: BDD match plus regular-expression path policies/automata described, but implementation reports only loop/blackhole invariant checker and what-if link analyzer. No policy-checker experiment or formal soundness/completeness theorem for the full checker. §4: Vendor PBR redirect can be modeled by cascading classifiers and connecting permit to redirect, deny to ordinary forwarding. Extra symbolic length/time fields can encode static conditions. Traffic statistics, mirroring, rate limiting and congestion avoidance are explicitly outside the model; stateful middlebox semantics not evaluated. §5.1: Around 5K Java/JDD lines; configuration parsers for three vendors, update parser for one, JSON intermediate form. Linux 3GHz Core i5/32GB. Microbenchmarks check loops after each update; threshold is 24h timeout or 32GB overflow. No end-to-end live-device detection-latency measurement. §5.1/Table 1: First three datasets generated using ONOS/Delta-net, not all production traces. Last five derive sequences from snapshots: insert ACL rules round-robin, then FIB rules round-robin, then delete in reverse. Purdue forwarding rules synthesized with shortest paths because original source has only ACLs. Such orders and synthesized routes limit workload representativeness. §5.1: AP Verifier modified for updates/loop checker; NetPlumber translated transfer-function rules with defaults preinserted and source per device. VeriFlow splits port ranges into prefixes. Delta-netMF is authors’ C++ multi-field extension using a multi-layer tree and explicitly may not be best extension. Java/C/C++ implementation differences and adaptations confound isolated algorithm comparisons. §5.2/Table 2: APKeep averages 6–127µs across eight datasets; at least 91.7% are under 250µs, rather than every update meeting a hard real-time bound. Pure-IP Delta-netMF often faster; disabling merges can improve small-partition workloads but costs on 4Switch/multi-field workloads. No worst-case guarantee derived from CDF. §5.3/Table 3/Figure 6: Failing methods’ Purdue EC counts show first 3,000 updates only. Stanford/Purdue Delta-netMF EC counts obtained by running creation-related functions despite full verifier failing. Counts/reduction percentages are not all completed end-to-end verification runs. §5.4/Table 4: Delta-net what-if numbers reused from prior paper on 3.47GHz Xeon; APKeep uses this paper’s 3GHz i5. Claimed 17×/93× loop-inclusive ratios are cross-machine measurements, not controlled same-host experiments. §5.5/Figure 7: Synthetic NAT rules choose edge-port predicates/prefixes and translate addresses; appended after forwarding rules. Prose names Stanford* and Purdue*, while Figure 7 labels Stanford* and Internet2. Prose says 0–20 NATs with 25 rules each yield 0–1000 rules, whereas arithmetic yields 0–500. Preserve ambiguity rather than silently assigning dataset or count. §7: Bootstrap fetches full state once, then requires sufficiently frequent updates. Asynchronously collected state can produce false alarms. Suspect-then-recheck time window is proposed with detailed design left to future work; no demonstrated solution for lost/reordered updates, device model fidelity or consistent global snapshot.     - what: Proves decidability and complexity results for termination, fair non-termination and fair starvation of dynamically spawning recursive threads under a fixed context-switch bound, introducing VASS with balloons as the key intermediate model. Ordinary termination reduces through downward closures to VASS non-termination, yielding the 2EXPSPACE result. Fairness is not downward-closure preserving, so VASS with balloons stores semi-linear multisets of future spawns; progressive runs and a shallow-run theorem reduce DCPS fair behavior to VASSB reachability, then to ordinary VASS reachability. - EEV BNN verification (2020)
    - title: Efficient Exact Verification of Binarized Neural Networks
    - what: Presents EEV, an exact (sound and complete) verifier for binarized neural networks. BNN layers compile to reified cardinality constraints; MiniSatCS adds native propagation for these constraints. BinMask induces balanced layer-wise sparsity, Cardinality Bound Decay (CBD) shrinks threshold bounds, and adaptive gradient cancelling trains networks whose exact robustness is tractable. The SAT encoding uses {0,1} activations, sparse {-1,0,1} weights, quantized inputs, thermometer-encoded perturbation intervals, and cached network clauses. The paper explains why balanced sparsity matters more than total sparsity and why lower cardinality bounds reduce sequential-counter encoding size, improve propagation, and make outputs predictable. Standard hard-tanh straight-through adversarial training can produce high PGD but low exact robustness; tanh/adaptive gradients and verifier-generated adversaries narrow this gap. EEV also encodes ensemble reject queries requiring all models to agree on the same wrong class.
    - number: MiniSatCS >100x over unmodified SAT
    - number: EEV total speedup 338.28–2440.65x vs real-valued exact verifier
    - number: BinMask solve 756.288→0.002s MNIST and 0.267→0.003s CIFAR10
    - number: CBD mean bound 148.3→2.7 MNIST; 123.8→2.1 CIFAR10
    - limits: Exactness applies to the quantized BNN and encoded infinity-norm perturbation domain, not arbitrary floating-point inference. Inputs are quantized (s=1/255 or 2epsilon), final batch normalization is restricted to scalar statistics, and verification remains NP-hard with timeouts for harder settings. Robustness/accuracy tradeoffs are severe on CIFAR10 at large epsilon; CBD can reduce natural accuracy. Results use MNIST/CIFAR10 architectures and do not prove properties of real-valued or distributed systems.

- Flow-CTL* Petri nets (2020)
    - title: Model Checking Branching Properties on Petri Nets with Transits (Full Version)
    - what: Introduces Flow-CTL* for branching properties of data-flow chains in Petri nets with transits, while retaining LTL assumptions for control fairness and maximality; reduces checking to ordinary Petri-net LTL model checking. Transit relations separate control tokens from data-flow chains. Flow-CTL* formulas combine flow-tree branching requirements with run-level control assumptions. The construction builds Büchi-automaton subnets, supports stuttering and activation tokens, and proves correctness of the reduction from a transit net and Flow-CTL* formula to a safe Petri net with inhibitor arcs and an LTL formula.

- Gauntlet: Finding Bugs in Compilers for Programmable Packet Processing (2020)
    - what: Gauntlet finds P4 compiler crashes with well-formed random programs, semantic mistakes in accessible compiler passes through SMT equivalence checking, and backend miscompilations through model-derived input/output packet tests. Its symbolic P4 interpreter supplies both oracles. The authors report96confirmed distinct bugs across P4C,BMv2 and Tofino over eight months,54fixed, and six specification changes. This is compiler bug finding with conditional translation validation of tested transformations, not verification of every compiler execution or correctness of the user network program. Captures generator probability/size controls, independent block semantics, symbolic table encoding and parameter directions, undefined-behavior taint and unstable-code distinction, parser/ToP4 dependencies, per-pass reparse/check workflow, constrained backend test generation and dropped-test limits. Preserves all bug status/location counts, timing rows, six concrete bug families, specification ambiguities, recent-merge count inconsistency, manual reduction and unmeasured coverage.
    - limits: §1–2: P4_16 finite bit-vector state and bounded/forbidden loops make equivalence decidable in principle. Control-flow loops are forbidden; parser loops are bounded by packet processing, so headline “no loops” should not be generalized to absence of every parser cycle. Efficient practical checks still depend on small programs and limited branching. This restriction distinguishes the method from unrestricted C; it is not an equivalence decision procedure for arbitrary Rust or distributed programs. §2.1/Table1: Crash bug means abnormal compiler termination without usable output/error, including assertion failure, segmentation fault,incomplete error and out-of-memory. Semantic bug means compiled behavior differs from input-program semantics, including packet outputs. Taxonomy levels1–7 are ASCII,words,syntax,type,static,dynamic,model conformity. Focus is static and higher-level failures rather than lexer/parser fuzzing alone. Some concrete failures reveal valid input incorrectly rejected; legality/specification uncertainty is resolved with developers. §2.2–2.3: Goal is many bugs, not completeness or a verified compiler. Differential testing across P4 targets cannot assume identical target semantics; independent same-target compilers were unavailable. Gauntlet tests mature P4C,BMv2,Tofino, excluding preliminary eBPF/uBPF/PSA toolchains. Its principal tests deliberately avoid target-specific extern calls. This is not a proof a particular P4 application satisfies network safety properties. §3/§5.2: Package parameters define input/output observables. Each programmable block is encoded separately; BMv2 v1model has Parser,VerifyChecksum,Ingress,Egress,ComputeChecksum,Deparser. out/inout form outputs; in/inout are symbolic inputs. Paths yield nested if-then-else expressions containing resulting parameter tuples. Copy-in is left-to-right; out values start uninitialized, and out/inout copy back on return. Correct interpretation of these effects is part of the trusted semantics. §4: Random generation grows a P4C IR AST probabilistically and emits P4 with ToP4. Node probabilities steer language coverage and keep programs small in lines/paths. A skeleton captures each target package/restrictions; two generator backends correspond to BMv2 and Tofino. Such warnings are not counted automatically as semantic bugs. §5.2: Interpreter took five months to become reliable enough for finding compiler semantic bugs. No machine configuration,repetitions,CI or solver-timeout rate for these timings is given. §7.3/Figure5a–c: Missing SideEffectOrdering transformation of ternary nested in addition crashes Tofino; missed InlineFunctions also leaks unsupported calls to backend. Unknown-width shift crashes type inference and prompts specification prohibition. A valid slice expression instead becomes illegal through StrengthReduction index overflow. These demonstrate source legality, downstream symptoms and originating faulty pass must be distinguished. §7.3/Figure5d: Passing low-byte slice as inout while assigning disjoint high-byte slice should preserve high-byte assignment. SimplifyDefUse assumed entire variable copied back and deleted the assignment. At least11/26P4C semantic bugs concern side effects/copy-in-copy-out;21/33P4C crash bugs involve type checker. - GSPACER (2020)
    - title: Global Guidance for Local Generalization in Model Checking
    - what: Adds explicit global guidance to local IC3-style lemma generation. Three general rules—implemented as GS PACER on top of Z3 SPACER—use the current lemma set to introduce blocking states/lemmas and mitigate locality failures. The paper specifies subsume, concretize, and conjecture mechanisms, instantiates them for Linear Integer Arithmetic with model-based projection and anti-unification, and compares interpolation-enabled and interpolation-free configurations. Global guidance preserves the IC3 architecture and can support non-linear CHCs/LRA in the implementation.

    - number: Best GS PACER configurations solve significantly more instances than every SPACER configuration; interpolation-off GS PACER is best on CHC-18 and only slightly worse on CHC-19
    - number: On PLDI18, GS PACER solved 284 safe/68 unsafe versus SPACER 216/68 and Linear Arbitrary 270/65

Results depend on CHC-COMP and artifact benchmark distributions and a 10-minute timeout on one CPU/memory setup. Authors note SMT runtime nondeterminism and leave theories lacking interpolation (e.g., bit-vectors) as future work.

- HYDRA distributed BMC (2020)
    - title: Distributed Bounded Model Checking
    - what: Presents HYDRA, an adaptive distributed BMC algorithm that dynamically unfolds call graphs and splits path sets into disjoint verification partitions farmed to cluster clients. It modifies Microsoft CORRAL, uses solver complexity to choose split points, and adapts split intervals to idle workers. A server coordinates partitions while clients run standard BMC; split decisions encode required/avoided control nodes, preserving completeness because any counterexample lies in one partition. HYDRA includes client backtracking, partition prioritization and solver-informed splitting, retaining SMT solvers as black boxes.
    - number: 32 clients achieve 20x speedup; mean 20.4x, median 9.7x
    - number: CORRAL solved 58 instances within 1000s; HYDRA solved substantially more (figure)
    - number: Experiments use 16 clients/server and split parameters delta_c=0.5s, K=20
    - number: Hard instances required at least 200s serial solving or timed out
    - limits: BMC is bounded by loop/recursion limits and proves only the encoded bound. Network/server coordination and partition overhead can dominate with few workers. Results target CORRAL/SDV C benchmarks and may not transfer to other languages or symbolic engines.

- Leaderless SMR ROLL limits (2020)
    - title: Leaderless State-Machine Replication: Specification, Properties, Limits
    - what: The paper gives a framework for leaderless state-machine replication (SMR), modeling dependency graphs, command phases, dependency discovery, consensus objects, and execution batches. It defines reliability, optimal latency, and load balancing (ROLL) properties and proves a trade-off: with n processes, fast-path quorum size n−F and failure tolerance f, ROLL protocols must satisfy 2F+f−1≤n. It further proves a lower bound on message delay for ROLL-optimal protocols, explaining the chaining effect seen in EPaxos. Generic SMR is shown to reduce to the leaderless abstraction, while cycles mean leaderless protocols need mutual dependency visibility rather than a total order.
    - limits: The model is wait-free asynchronous message passing with fail-stop failures, unbounded logs/commands, deterministic state machines, and a conflict relation that safely over-approximates non-commutativity. Correctness is expressed by validity, stability, and consistency of dependency graphs; liveness and implementation details are abstracted. The supplied text contains the framework and introductory definitions but not the later full proof pages, so numerical lower-bound derivations beyond the stated inequality and the complete §4–§8 argument cannot be independently quoted from this extraction.

- Lexicographic stochastic games (2020)
    - title: Stochastic Games with Lexicographic Reachability-Safety Objectives
    - what: Studies finite turn-based zero-sum stochastic games whose ordered objectives are reachability or safety, and computes the lexicographic value and optimal strategies. For absorbing targets, removes locally suboptimal actions and characterizes optimality as local lex-optimality plus almost-sure reachability of a final set. It reduces safety objectives to quantified reachability, then handles non-absorbing targets by recursively solving stages for visited target sets (up to 2^n−1), composing stage strategies with n-bit memory. It proves determinacy, deterministic strategies with at most 2^n−1 memory classes, PSPACE-hardness and an NEXPTIME∩coNEXPTIME upper bound (NP∩coNP for constant n or absorbing objectives).
    - number: Dice[50]: 96,295 states, 3 s lex solve; Hallway 10x10: 400,000 states, 548 s; Avoid Observer 20x20: 1,436,404 states, 281 s; stages used 1/3 for Dice and 4/7 for AV; all instances solved within minutes on 2.4 GHz quad-core i5 with 4 GB Java VM
    - limits: Finite state, turn-based stochastic games with Borel reachability/safety objectives; values use lexicographic sup-inf and the algorithm relies on a single-objective solver (experiments use approximate PRISM-games value iteration, so exact lex-values are not measured). General-case complexity leaves a PSPACE-vs-NEXPTIME gap; only reachability/safety are treated, and parity or richer quantitative objectives are future work.

- Local Reasoning About the Presence of Bugs: Incorrectness Separation Logic (2020)
    - what: Incorrectness separation logic combines under-approximate reachability triples with separation logic’s frame rule. Owning an invalidated location as a negative heap resource prevents unsound framing after deallocation. The paper states logic soundness, a footprint characterization covering successful and erroneous executions, and soundness of a begin-anywhere symbolic execution calculus. Pulse illustrates bounded path pruning and inferred heap assumptions; its practical call-skipping mode has weaker guarantees than the calculus. Distinguishes a satisfiable error result reachable from some inferred local state from whole-program reachability, all-path correctness, or a failed proof. Explains the negative-heap counterexample, domain monotonicity, reversed consequence/bi-abduction entailments, error reporting without assuming the error, optional allocation-reuse pruning, and the explicit gap between sound intra-procedural rules and heuristic treatment of calls. Preserves all reported experimental counts and the limits of fixes as evidence.
    - limits: §§2–4: [p] C [epsilon:q] means every q state is reached from some p state via a finite C execution with that exit. It does not say every p state reaches q or that every run terminates. A false q makes any such triple vacuous; an erroneous triple establishes bug existence only with a satisfiable result. Inferred p is a local environment assumption, not a proof that main or any real caller reaches it. §1 p227: no-false-positive logic guarantee is conditional on the model assumptions; the authors explicitly separate these from whether running code satisfies them. This is a semantic theorem, not a machine-checked implementation guarantee or universal empirical zero-false-positive claim for all Pulse configurations. §3/Fig4: language has infinite values, finitely many variables, standard interpreted expressions, nondeterministic choice/havoc/finite iteration, assume, local variables, labeled explicit errors and heap allocation/free/load/store. Labels are unique. No concurrency, network, message passing, fairness or infinite-trace liveness semantics is supplied. Procedure calls are not a primitive in this calculus; examples use given models/inlining. §§3–4/Figs5–6: heap is a finite partial map from locations to values or a distinguished deallocated marker bottom. A missing location is unknown, while a bottom-marked location is owned and known deallocated. Neither may be silently equated with the other. Two separated resources cannot own the same location, including two negative resources. Deallocation retains its domain entry; allocation may use an absent or deallocated location. §3/Fig5 and §4/Fig6: FreeNull treats free(null) as an error. Reader comparison with ordinary C semantics: C free(NULL) is a no-op, so this toy-language rule needs a matching translation/model before using its error result as a claim about C code. The paper’s C/C++ motivation is not a complete source-language semantics; pointer arithmetic, undefined behavior, allocation layout, integers and library contracts are not fully formalized. §3: frame requires mod(C) disjoint from free variables of the frame. Consequence weakens the presumption and strengthens the result, reversing Hoare implication directions. Choice may select one branch; loop rules describe finite paths, and early errors short-circuit sequential composition. Standard backward SL rules are generally invalid here. Store/Free rules quantify over an arbitrary old value, rather than merely an existentially unknown old value, to retain usable under-approximate specifications. §4/Theorem1: derivable ISL triples are semantically valid. The chapter states this theorem but refers full proofs of all theorems to separate technical appendix [38]. No proof-assistant checking or verified Pulse implementation is reported here. §4.1/Theorem2: the entire denotational relation equals framing the footprint relation; footprint pairs include only memory accessed along that particular successful or erroneous execution. The result follows from heap-domain monotonicity with negative resources, is a property of the model rather than under-approximate syntax, and could also benefit over-approximate logic using that model. Full footprint function appears only in the separate appendix. §4.2: a naive over-approximate post inclusion alone does not justify the standard frame rule; fault avoidance or explicit frame preservation is needed. ISL instead uses simple under-approximate post inclusion and includes unsafe-state footprints. This comparison concerns the stated semantic models; it is not a claim that existing sound SL tools lack frame reasoning. §5/Fig8: symbolic heaps omit inductive predicates; loops are bounded by Nloops and paths at each program point by Ndisjuncts. Pruning preserves under-approximate soundness but can miss bugs. No joins or widening are needed for this bounded exploration; no completeness beyond these explored/modelled paths is established. Bounded decidability is described as likely under decidable Boolean conditions, not a proved theorem. §5/SymbExec: with previously valid [p0] C0 [ok:q0] and primitive [p] C [epsilon:q], find missing M and frame F satisfying p*F entails q0*M. Frame M through C0 (mod(C0) disjoint fv(M)), frame F through C (mod(C) disjoint fv(F)), then compose. This reverses the ordinary SL bi-abduction direction. It can extend inferred initial assumptions along a chosen branch without a second all-path re-execution. §5 p243: practical error rules require no missing M and require current state to force the fault, using entailment in both directions with an appropriate frame. They do not invent a dangling/null assumption solely to report an error on a bare dereference. This is a chosen reporting policy in addition to logical under-approximation, not a complete bug detector. §5 p244: formalized analysis is intra-procedural; function-call summaries remain future work. Practical call skipping assumes no effect except fresh nondeterministic return/reference-parameter values and may introduce both false positives and false negatives. Hence theorem3 must not be applied unqualified to this deployed mode, or to arbitrary library models. §5 p245: Pulse omits Alloc2 (reuse), assumes distinct memory unless known aliases, bounds paths/loops, and uses selected under-approximate library models (vector push_back always reallocates). These prune feasible modeled behaviors; their soundness assumes the selected behavior really is possible under relevant library/input conditions. They do not prove every push_back invalidates existing pointers. §5 evaluation: OpenSSL1.0.2d has8681 functions and yields zero reports in6s on24 Linux cores. Proprietary C++ corpus has hundreds of thousands of procedures and17 reports, without per-report validation or a ground-truth bug denominator.     - what: Classifies parameterized complexity of model checking (MC), satisfiability (SAT), and exact-team-size satisfiability (m-SAT) for propositional dependence logic (PDL). The table leaves m-SAT under formula-treewidth and split count unresolved.

    - title: SAW: A Tool for Safety Analysis of Weakly-Hard Systems
    - what: Presents SAW, a tool for infinite-time safety verification of general nonlinear weakly-hard systems under (m,K) deadline constraints. Algorithm 2 labels edges by deadline meet/miss and discards grids whose Flow* overapproximation intersects the unsafe set.     - what: Combines an efficient HLC γ-extension filter with an accurate SMT predicate detector. - Molinari interval model checking thesis (2019)
    - title: Model Checking: the Interval Way
    - what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval temporal logic (HS) over finite Kripke structures and timeline-based system models. It proves decidability and EXPSPACE hardness for full homogeneous HS, classifies many fragments, compares interval and point logics, studies regular-expression extensions, and derives timed-automata procedures for timeline planning and MITL model checking. The thesis builds BEk descriptors for a nonelementary decidability procedure, reductions proving EXPSPACE hardness, and fragment-specific small-model/oracle/automata algorithms ranging through PSPACE and bounded-query polynomial hierarchy classes. It compares HS variants with LTL, CTL, and CTL* under homogeneous semantics, then relaxes homogeneity using regular expressions while preserving or increasing fragment complexity. For dense-time timelines, unrestricted planning is undecidable; simple future trigger rules are decidable via timed automata, with EXPSPACE completeness for non-singular intervals and PSPACE completeness for intervals in Intv(0,∞). MITL model checking reduces inclusion to timed-automata emptiness.

    - title: Robustness Verification of Tree-based Models
    - what: Develops exact and anytime lower-bound verification for decision-tree ensembles under l∞ perturbations. - Lazy Self-composition for Security Verification. (2018)
    - what: Combines symbolic path-sensitive taint analysis of one program copy with precise two-copy safety verification to avoid eager full self-composition. Ifc-CEGAR validates candidate taint leaks, transfers relational invariant information and refines taint updates. Ifc-BMC duplicates only possibly tainted computations while unrolling, and can prove safety early when all live initial taint disappears. SeaHorn prototypes are compared to eager composition on small security benchmarks. Details observability/declassification predicates, the one-sided meaning of taint, proof-trace rewriting versus strengthening and the model refinement needed to restore induction. Keeps conditional completeness separate from prototype support; preserves no-fresh-secret condition for BMC termination, unknown handling, bitvector/struct limitations, all benchmark values and the narrow evidence behind scalability/constant-time claims.
    - limits: §§3–4: transition-system variables and quantifier-free first-order theory formulas describe Init, Tr and Bad. Tr is assumed reflexive so either program copy may stutter. H identifies initially secret variables and L is its complement. Security is defined relative to the chosen operational model and observation predicates, not every possible timing/cache/network observation. §4: Obs_x specifies when a low variable is adversary-observable. The terminal-output policy, concurrently executing observers and selected declassification contexts are modeled by these predicates. Setting Obs false or explicitly marking a value untainted changes the permitted policy and must be justified externally; it is not a derived no-leak theorem. §4.1: taint marks high variables true and low variables false initially. Theta(expression) disjoins taint of its variables; conditional update taint includes condition taint and the chosen branch expression. It tracks explicit and implicit flows but overapproximates value dependence, e.g. different expressions with the same result. The final prose reverses x1/x2 dependency direction; the displayed update gives the intended meaning. §4.2: self-composition starts low variables equal and leaves high values independent. Bad requires one low value unequal while both copies satisfy its observation predicate. Results concern this paired-execution definition under the chosen stuttering model; termination behavior or microarchitectural leakage is not automatically covered. §5 Corollaries1–2: real self-composition leaks imply possible taint leaks; no taint leak proves no modeled leak. A tainted output alone does not prove insecurity. Untainted implies equality across the related copies, whereas equality need not imply untainted in the original abstraction. §5.1 Algorithm1: taint solver SAFE ends the check; a taint counterexample triggers a constrained self-composed problem. One described Constraint choice bounds all self-composed executions by the counterexample length k rather than merely replaying one control path. An actual paired witness gives UNSAFE; a spurious one supplies relational facts for refinement. §5.1: ReWrite adds single-copy facts and entailed equalities/disequalities while preserving claimed inductive traces, without itself improving the taint abstraction. Strengthening additionally uses proved equalities to require no taint, which can destroy induction. Refine changes selected next-taint functions under the strengthened frame condition to restore induction; it is not merely adding an unproved invariant to the original model. §5.1 Theorem1 assumes a sound and complete first-order-theory model checker maintaining inductive traces. It states Ifc-CEGAR soundness/completeness under that assumption and gives a proof sketch, not unconditional decidability or termination for arbitrary C/CHCs or a proof that Spacer always terminates. Lemma claims/trace transformations are not mechanically verified here. §5.1 printed formula issues, visually confirmed: equations10/12 initialize a trace over Y=X∪Xt using Init_d, which is defined over X∪Xd; displayed component-preservation implications on p.145 use frame i on both sides instead of i+1; equation13 switches superscript d to s. The record follows the stated algorithmic intent without silently treating the typeset formulas as a complete executable correctness proof. §5.2 Algorithms2–3: an UNSAT taint query permits the duplicate value to reuse the original computation. SAT or UNKNOWN conservatively duplicates it. At BND without a conclusive result return UNKNOWN; failure to find a bounded counterexample alone is not safety. The simplified bad formula omits Obs only for exposition. §§1,5.2: early safety requires no live variable tainted and no leak found in the checked prefix. Initial secret taint must be exhausted and no new secret input introduced later; the introduction explicitly states this assumption and says later tainted inputs need a modified check. Does not provide a general finite completeness bound for ongoing distributed services. Algorithm notation issues: Algorithm2 calls LazySC(M,Mt), whereas Algorithm3 header orders(Mt,M); Algorithm1 advertises UNKNOWN but main loop has no solver-UNKNOWN branch, and its UNKNOWN return follows until-infinity. These are high-level sketches; practical resource/solver-unknown handling is not completely specified. Algorithm2 also does not explicitly distinguish an unknown composed-property query before its early-safety check. §§6–6.2: prototype initially described as not bit-precise and not supporting complex lists. More specifically CEGAR uses LLVM instrumentation plus Spacer and cannot handle benchmark structs or bitvector operations; BMC works over CHCs with Z3 and handles all evaluated programs. Do not generalize CEGAR restrictions to the list/BV BMC rows or infer full C bit-precise semantics from them. §§6.2–6.4: Intel Core i7-4578U,8GB RAM;300s timeout. Eager comparisons use the same backend on two copies. All seven CEGAR rows are safe, only pwdcheck2 needs one refinement; the other six are discharged by taint analysis with no self-composition refinement. Eight BMC rows include two unsafe variants. These selected small/microbenchmarks are not a large deployed-code security audit. §6.4: Table3 runtime at array size64 is85.44s, supporting under2min on that instance. Author statement of exponential runtime growth is a qualitative characterization of eight observations, not a proved asymptotic bound or scaling to unbounded arrays. Exact BND values, program sizes, solver versions, repetition variance and memory consumption are not supplied. §§7–8: security-type, dynamic-taint and product-program comparisons are discussion claims without separate head-to-head benchmark data here. General k-safety and quantified relational invariants for unbounded data structures are future work. No verified implementation, certificate validation, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM evaluation is reported. Frontend, instrumentation, policy and solvers remain trusted.

    - what: Compares local labels, one shared global proof, and mixed proofs for constant-radius distributed verification, quantifying the cost of distributing global evidence. Uniform local proofs yield Θ(n) price; At-most-one-selected (Amos) has O(log n) uniform labels and Θ(n) price. Minimum Spanning Tree has O(log²n) local proofs and O(n log n) global proof, giving Θ(log n). At-least-one-selected requires Ω(n log n) mixed proof, and reversing decision therefore needs Ω(log n) local or Ω(n log n) global evidence. A block-neighborhood counting argument supplies the lower bound and is lifted to leader election, spanning tree and odd-cycle. Bipartite global proofs are conjectured Θ(n log n), with bounds depending on identifier range. The paper connects local/global nondeterministic hierarchies to communication-complexity hierarchies.

- POS concurrency sampling (2018)
    - title: Partial Order Aware Concurrency Sampling
    - what: Presents POS, a randomized concurrency scheduler that samples partial orders rather than redundant total interleavings. It assigns random priorities to events, executes the highest-priority enabled event, and reassigns priorities of events racing with the executed event. The paper formalizes sequentially consistent concurrent machines, event independence, partial-order equivalence and minimum partial-order coverage probability. BasicPOS uses immutable priorities but suffers propagated constraints; POS versions priorities by per-object access counts, yielding bipartite constraints and a theorem with a race-count-dependent lower bound. Implementation supports read-only-event relaxation and a periodic priority reset workaround for busy loops. Micro benchmarks use 16 events across four threads/objects; macro tests use SCTBench and Maple, with explicit exclusions and conservative geometric-mean handling.

    - limits: The machine model assumes sequential consistency, each statement accesses at most one shared object, disabled events eventually enable, and executions terminate (finite traces). POS needs a race predicate and probabilistic priorities; fairness is probabilistic and implementation resets priorities every 10^3 voluntary context switches, with claimed minimal effect. Guarantees are lower bounds on partial-order coverage, not exhaustive testing; read-only relaxation depends on correctly classifying races.

- Verifying concurrent software using movers in Cspec (2018)
    - what: Cspec is a Coq framework for implementing and proving concurrent systems through state-machine refinement, composable layers and reusable proof patterns. Right/left movers reduce interleavings to atomic execution of larger code blocks. Fully mechanized patterns verify a Maildir-like server, Cmail, and a locked counter over an x86-TSO model. Extracted Haskell Cmail scales on a twelve-core tmpfs benchmark. Records state/argument-dependent commutation and stable enablement, finite-prefix safety scope, protocol proof obligations, error-state elimination, zero-effect retries and partition lifting. Captures six concrete mail concurrency cases, conservative PID-filtered directory listing, two naming plans, all TSO layers and the previous-owner buffer invariant. Saves all framework/layer LOC and pattern counts, measured setup, development anecdotes and precise trusted boundaries.
    - limits: §§1,5,7: Programs, operation/state definitions, implementations, abstraction relations, invariants and proofs are written manually within Cspec/Coq; it cannot directly verify arbitrary existing software. Executables use Coq extraction to Haskell (OCaml is mentioned as an alternative). The result is not a proof of arbitrary compiled C, Rust or a native binary. §§5.2,7: Correctness is trace inclusion, with every finite prefix representing possibly infinite behavior. Only safety properties are targeted. No scheduler fairness, termination, starvation freedom, eventual successful delivery or lock acquisition follows. The proof may insert a never-executed stably enabled left-mover into an equivalent execution; it does not make the actual scheduler run it. §§1–2,8.6: Node failures are outside scope. File-system crash behavior and durability are not proved despite the Maildir motivation. Top-level intended behavior and bottom-level file-system model must be correct. Coq soundness and standard assumptions including functional extensionality, extraction/runtime, driver and concrete syscall mapping are trusted. §§1,5.3,8: SMTP/POP3 parsing and protocol implementation are unverified. The Haskell network/file-system driver lies outside the proof. Compatibility with Go SMTP, postal and rabid is testing, not protocol conformance proof. TLS, spam filtering and logging are absent. §6.1 Figures 10–12: Commutation must preserve both operations’ individual return values and final state across distinct PIDs. Atomic blocks have right-movers, at most one non-mover, then left-movers. State-dependent properties need only hold after the already-executed prefix but require proofs for all reachable modeled states, not sampled interleavings. §6.1: Disabled intermediate operations require stable enablement when moving an operation earlier: enablement survives undoing another process’s step. An existing locked-file read can be a left-mover although reading arbitrary newly created/temporary files is not. Lock ownership rules must ensure other processes cannot release this process’s lock. §6.2: Protocol semantics disables forbidden operations, such as unlocked accesses. Sound use requires proving every API user follows the protocol under unrestricted semantics. Merely restricting the environment would assume away the race; Cspec requires the refinement proof. §6.3 Figure 13: The abstraction pattern keeps operation types fixed, preserves the return value and relates successor states for every low-level step. Invariant introduction uses an identity relation. An absorbing abstract error state can relate to any low-level state, but a later protocol proof must show it unreachable before obtaining the final guarantee. §6.4: Retry-loop bodies must either perform the correct successful effect and exit, or have zero effect and retry. This supports a safety/atomicity proof without guaranteeing eventual success. Partition lifting requires proven single-shard refinement plus correct naming and disjoint decomposition at top and bottom. §§3–5 Figures 1,3,6: The displayed mail/file-system specifications permit a false delivery/link return with no effect, not solely a proved name-collision cause. They are permissive safety specifications and do not guarantee success. The paper uses atomic rename terminology later; earlier implementation/spec uses link followed by unlink, with no destination overwrite, so do not substitute unrestricted POSIX rename semantics. §8.1: With concurrent deletion, PID-filtered readdir deliberately permits a superset of existing names. It is a right-mover, not a both-mover, in that case. A name absent from the superset is free; a reported name need not still exist. Plan 2 describes random names but concretely uses the current timestamp and relies on retry rather than guaranteed collision freedom. §8.2 Figure 16: The x86-TSO case verifies a modeled counter built over shared memory and per-core store buffers. Any core may flush any portion of its buffer at each low-level operation. This is not validation of a physical processor, compiler memory model or executable counter benchmark. §8.3 Figure 17: Performance uses local simulated SMTP/POP3 requests on Linux tmpfs, avoiding network and persistent-storage bottlenecks. Authors implemented the unverified GoMail comparator. Request mix is 1:1 delivery versus read/delete over 100 random users. Message sizes, measurement durations, repetitions, error bars and raw runs are not supplied. §8.4 Figure 18: Effort is two people about six months part time, following another twelve months of failed alternative designs. Incremental deletion/naming/multi-user timings are author anecdotes, not controlled studies or independent replications. The text’s approximate 100–200 spec LOC per layer omits displayed extremes 63 and 323. §8.5 Figure 19: Proof-pattern counts are module uses and need not equal numbers of layers. The Cmail diagram describes naming plan 1; the count table also includes the retry pattern used in plan 2, which has one additional intermediate layer. §§2,8.6: The state-machine approach draws on TLA and I/O automata, but the work is not a TLA+ implementation/proof or a distributed node-failure theorem. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM-generated-specification/proof evaluation. Public artifact URL is recorded but not fetched or replayed.

- CEGIS digital controller synthesis (2017)
    - title: Automated Formal Synthesis of Digital Controllers for State-Space Physical Plants
    - what: Synthesizes safe finite-precision state-feedback controllers for discretized linear time-invariant plants. A CEGIS loop combines stability-constrained controller search with either multi-stage bounded verification up to a completeness threshold or abstraction/refinement with abstract acceleration and explicit quantization/noise bounds. The paper models ADC/DAC, fixed-point arithmetic, plant representation and rounding errors as bounded nondeterministic noise and interval operations. The baseline synthesizes on one initial state, then checks all hypercube vertices, precision soundness and a stability-derived completeness threshold; convexity proves vertex sufficiency. The abstraction backend accelerates all closed-loop powers into an infinite reach-tube, returns iteration/initial-state counterexamples, and refines eigenvalue constraints. Worked examples show successive counterexamples and precision increases; ten control benchmarks compare both backends.
    - number: controller fixed point Ic=8,Fc=8
    - number: 10 benchmarks, one-hour per-benchmark timeout
    - number: abstraction median 1.4 s vs multi-stage 9.4 s
    - number: abstraction solves 9 vs multi-stage 8
    - limits: Plants are controllable LTI ODEs with full state observation, discretized at a fixed sampling rate; synthesis targets zero reference, bounded hypercube initial states/inputs, SISO benchmarks and box safety. Stability/eigenvalue and completeness arguments assume suitable nonrepeated eigenvalues and asymptotic convergence. Fixed-point precision choices, discretization heuristics and abstraction refinement can cause timeouts or UNSAT despite a possible controller; safety beyond boxes or complex temporal objectives is not addressed. Results may not generalize beyond the selected benchmarks and output-based/continuous-time control is future work.

- Decorated-component synthesis (2017)
    - title: Look for the Proof to Find the Program: Decorated-Component-Based Program Synthesis
    - what: Introduces decorated-component-based synthesis (DCoS), which searches for a straight-line program and a bounded proof in a user-defined alternate semantics. Decorations add existential proof variables and can replace an expensive universal correctness check by an existential constraint when they abstract the concrete semantics.
    - number: 27 polynomial coefficients per program variable in the quadratic multiplication decoration
    - number: Table 1: search spaces approximately 10^9 to 2×10^25 and synthesis times about 1–50 s
    - number: ∃∀ block-cipher synthesis ~100 s versus ∃∃ ~1 s; hundreds of variants under 5 min
    - number: 30 secure-multiplication sketch variants
    - limits: Programs are bounded straight-line sketches; loops and richer proof systems are left as future work. The ∃∃ reduction is sound only when the decoration is a genuine abstraction and its alternate postcondition implies the concrete one; arbitrary decorations can encode useful nonfunctional filters but do not prove functional correctness. Security checks are deliberately sufficient and incomplete: the OT examples require posterior security verification. Human intuition is still needed to choose a proof domain and decorations, and unsatisfiable large families may scale poorly.

- Developing Bug-Free Machine Learning Systems With Formal Mathematics (2017)
    - what: Presents Certigrad, an implementation of stochastic computation graphs in Lean, with a reported machine-checkable proof that stochastic backpropagation produces unbiased estimates of the mathematical gradient of expected cost. It demonstrates a workflow in which formal specifications and attempted proofs guide implementation and expose both code errors and missing assumptions. It also reports verified Gaussian integration/reparameterization optimizations and an MNIST variational-autoencoder experiment with performance comparable to TensorFlow. Separates an executable stochastic program from its mathematical expectation semantics using Dist n, built by primitive sampling, deterministic returns and composition. The paper gives expectation and RNG-threading equations for each constructor. The initial all-graphs unbiasedness specification is strengthened with WellFormed, GradsExist, IntegralsExist and CanDiffUnderInts preconditions. A simple single-parameter, nonmemoizing implementation is proved first; a multi-parameter memoizing implementation is then proved equivalent. A heuristic tactic proves model-specific preconditions for the transformed AEVB graph. The verified optimization sequence integrates Gaussian KL terms and replaces parameter-dependent Gaussian sampling with standard-normal sampling followed by scale/shift, preserving the objective while changing the gradient estimator.
    - limits: Correctness is relative to the stated mathematical specification and adopted axioms. The authors assume real numbers, integration and primitive mathematical laws rather than constructing their foundations. They report repairing initially unsound axioms by restoring integrability conditions, but this reading does not independently audit that axiom set. The final displayed scalar theorem requires unique node identifiers and scalar leaves (WellFormed), appropriate differentiability for all relevant stochastic choices (GradsExist), existence of integrals (IntegralsExist), and conditions allowing gradients through integrals (CanDiffUnderInts). The implementation is reported to handle arbitrary tensor shapes and multiple parameters; the displayed specification deliberately simplifies these. Proving the generic algorithm is insufficient for an arbitrary client graph: each graph must meet the preconditions. Some are undecidable in general, so the theorem-proving tactic is heuristic rather than a complete decision procedure. The proof concerns ideal infinite-precision real arithmetic. The authors explicitly say replacing reals with floating-point numbers technically invalidates the specification and may cause numerical instability; no floating-point error bound is established here. The running system trusts optimized Eigen tensor operations and a small C++ wrapper to match the formally reasoned operations, and relies on Lean VM/runtime and primitive pseudo-random sampling. The paper describes corresponding mathematical/procedural distribution interpretations but does not establish a checked correctness theorem for the concrete RNG, Eigen, C++ wrapper or execution platform. Unbiased stochastic gradients do not establish convergence of ADAM, bounded gradient variance, statistical validity, good generalization or model fit. The empirical AEVB training comparison addresses one example, not those general guarantees. The source repeatedly says proving exposes all implementation errors. The supported guarantee is absence of violations of the modeled specification under its assumptions; specification errors, inconsistent axioms and implementation layers outside the model remain material, as the paper itself discusses. Claims of reduced cognitive burden and finding all bugs early are the authors’ development experience, not a controlled developer study or complete empirical bug census. The paper reports increased overall workload but supplies no person-hour or proof-size measurements.

- Dijkstra Monads for Free (2017)
    - what: The paper derives a weakest-precondition generator automatically from a simple definition of an effect such as state or exceptions. A weakest precondition is the least that must hold before code runs for its result to be correct. With this, F* can generate proof obligations for Z3.
    - number: no experiments, runtimes or proof sizes reported
    - number: No success rate, runtime, proof size or person-hours reported
    - number: Examples: state increment, division with exceptions, rollback state, dynamic allocation, information flow, continuations
    - limits: It is sound for total correctness (the code terminates and is right) in the paper's calculus. Humans write the specification. In the functional-interpretation route it works only for terminating code. An information-flow policy needs a separate argument.

- DiVM: Model Checking with LLVM and Graph Memory (2017)
    - what: Presents DiVM, an LLVM-IR virtual machine with graph-organized memory and verification hypercalls, plus DiOS, a verification-oriented OS that supports POSIX-like C/C++ programs in explicit-state and abstraction-driven model checking. The VM represents heap objects as graph nodes linked by pointer edges, tracks pointer/definedness types in shadow memory, uses object-level allocation/free and stable object identifiers, and stores stacks as graph-linked activation frames. A small hypercall interface exposes nondeterministic choice, interrupt points, tracing, shared-object marking and machine control to a virtualized OS. This separation lets the verifier keep a simple initial/successor interface while the OS implements scheduling, threads, syscalls, monitors and faults. The paper explains τ and symmetry reductions, abstraction compatibility, and evaluates DIVINE 4 against DIVINE 3 and ESBMC.
    - number: DIVINE 4 runs 926 error-free models (from 1,045 total: 926 correct and 119 erroneous) in 8:15:44 and explores 33.0 million states.
    - number: Compared with DIVINE 3 on 457 models, DIVINE 4 takes 1:05:17 versus 7:00:33 and explores 4.729 million versus 11.6 million states.
    - number: Against modified DIVINE 3 on 448 models, DIVINE 4 takes 29:27 versus 5:01:40 and explores 1.820 million versus 5.803 million states.
    - number: ESBMC comparison covers 60 models: DIVINE 4 takes 10:22 versus ESBMC 2:43:39.
    - limits: The target is mainly C/C++ units with no uncontrolled external input; scheduling and failures are nondeterministic, while malloc/new are assumed non-failing for most benchmarks. Runtime typing is required because LLVM memory is untyped and casts defeat static recovery. Pointer-to-number conversions can invalidate heap canonicalization, so noncanonical state forms must be retained for successor generation. IPC/shared-memory pointers need OS translation to preserve isolation. Evaluation is explicit-state and depends on DiOS/library coverage; comparisons expose DIVINE 3 omissions and ESBMC's limited C++ support.
